Sources: Wikipedia, Chromium, Epic Games, Unreal Engine, NASA/JPL, Ingenuity

Before Operating Systems

  • 1940s–1950s: switches, punch cards, raw code
  • One program controlled the whole machine
  • Devices, stop/start handled manually
  • Very slow, error-prone

Bell Labs and AT&T

  • Bell Labs was the research arm of AT&T (founded 1925).
  • In the late 1960s, they needed an operating system to manage computers for communication networks (manage = schedule programs, allocate CPU & memory, control devices, share files).
  • 1969–1971: Led to the creation of UNIX as a flexible system for research and telecom needs.

History of C/C++

  • Early 1970s at Bell Labs (Dennis Ritchie)
  • System programming for UNIX

Why C?

  • Close to hardware, portable
  • Small runtime, fast compilation

Questions?

From Code to Machine

C Code


    int totalCredits(int a, int b) {
        return a + b;
    }

Compiler


    $ gcc -S totalCredits.c -o totalCredits.s

Translates C source into assembly

Assembly


    totalCredits:
        mov eax, edi    ; a into eax
        add eax, esi    ; add b to eax
        ret             ; return result

x86-64 System V calling convention

Assembler


    $ as totalCredits.s -o totalCredits.o

Assembles into machine code (object file)

Machine Code


    55                ; push rbp
    89 f8             ; mov eax, edi
    01 f0             ; add eax, esi
    5d                ; pop rbp
    c3                ; ret

Compiled with gcc -O1 on x86-64

Enroll Student (C Code)


    #include <stdio.h>
    // Enroll a student
    void enroll_student() {
        printf("Linking...\n");
        printf("Enrolled!\n");
    }
    int main() {
        enroll_student();
        return 0;
    }

History of C++

C Is a Subset of C++

Every valid C program is (almost) valid C++

Why C++?

  • Object‑oriented programming
  • Performance with abstraction

Which is a subset of the other?

Variables

History of the Variable

  • 1957: FORTRAN adds named data
  • 1958: ALGOL adds := for it
  • Every language has kept it

Why Variables?

  • Store a value, reuse it
  • Give data a name

    // No var, repeat
    cout << 15;
    cout << 15;

    // Reuse the variable
    int credits = 15;
    cout << credits;
    cout << credits;

What Is a Variable?

  • A named spot in memory
  • Holds one value at a time
  • The value can change

Anatomy of a Variable

  • Type: what kind of value
  • Name: how you refer to it
  • Value: what's stored now

    int credits = 15;
    // ^    ^        ^
    // type name    value

Word Origin: "Variable"

  • Latin: variare, to change
  • Math: an unknown quantity
  • 1957: FORTRAN's named data

Declaring a Variable

  • Tells the compiler: this name
  • exists, and holds this type
  • No value yet

    int credits;
    // no value yet

Word Origin: "Declare"

  • Latin: declarare, make clear
  • You're telling the compiler
  • "this name will exist"

Code It: Declare a Variable

  • Declare an int named year
  • No value yet
  • How would you write it?

    int year;

Initializing a Variable

  • Declare AND give a value
  • Happens in one statement
  • Best practice: always do this

    int credits = 15;
    // declared & set

Word Origin: "Initialize"

  • Latin: initium, a beginning
  • "Set the starting value"
  • Happens at declaration

Quick Check

What's the difference: declare vs. initialize?

  1. No difference at all
  2. Initialize also sets a value
  3. Declare also sets a value

B. Initializing = declaring + giving it a starting value.

Code It: Initialize a Variable

  • Initialize gpa to 3.5
  • Type: double
  • How would you write it?

    double gpa = 3.5;

Assigning a Value

  • = is the assignment operator
  • Stores a value in a variable
  • Variable must exist first

    int credits;
    credits = 15;
    // after declare

Word Origin: "Assign"

  • Latin: assignare, mark out
  • 1958: ALGOL's := operator
  • C++ shortens it to just =

Code It: Assign a Value

  • Declare age (int) first
  • Then assign it 20
  • How would you write it?

    int age;
    age = 20;

Reassigning a Variable

  • Change the stored value
  • Old value is overwritten
  • Same variable, new value

    int credits = 15;
    credits = 18;
    // old value gone

Word Origin: "Reassign"

  • Latin: re-, again + assign
  • "Assign a new value again"
  • Same variable, new value

Quick Check

What happens when you reassign a variable?

  1. A new variable is created
  2. The old value is overwritten
  3. Nothing, it's an error

B. Reassigning overwrites the old value in place.

Code It: Reassign a Variable

  • credits starts at 12
  • Reassign it to 16
  • How would you write it?

    int credits = 12;
    credits = 16;

Declare, Initialize, Assign, Reassign

  • int x; is declaring
  • int x = 5; is initializing
  • x = 9; is (re)assigning

    int x; // declare
    x = 5; // assign
    int y = 5; // init
    y = 9; // reassign

Types of Variables

Why Do Types Matter?

  • Type = what kind of data
  • Sets the size in memory
  • Sets what operations work

Word Origin: "Type"

  • Greek: typos, a mark/model
  • Defines a value's shape
  • int, double, char, bool...

Operators: + and -

  • + adds two values
  • - subtracts two values
  • Work like in math class

    int a = 10, b = 3;
    int sum=a+b; // 13
    int diff=a-b; // 7

Operators: * and /

  • * multiplies two values
  • / divides two values
  • Division can drop decimals

    int a = 10, b = 3;
    int prod=a*b; // 30
    int quot=a/b; // 3

Type: int

  • Whole numbers only
  • No decimal point
  • e.g., credits, a count

    int credits = 15;
    int year = 2026;

int in Practice

  • Most common numeric type
  • No fractions allowed
  • 9/2 gives 4, not 4.5

    int a = 9;
    int b = 2;
    int result = a / b;
    cout << result; // 4

Quick Check

Which university variable fits int best?

  1. unitsCompleted
  2. cumulativeGPA
  3. studentEmail

A. unitsCompleted is a whole number, no decimals.

Code It: Units Completed

  • Declare units
  • Set it to 45
  • How would you write it?

    int units=45;

Type: double

  • Numbers with decimals
  • "Double precision" float
  • e.g., gpa, price, average

    double gpa = 3.8;
    double price = 19.99;

double in Practice

  • Keeps the decimal part
  • Use for any fraction
  • 9.0 / 2 gives 4.5

    double a = 9.0;
    double b = 2.0;
    double r = a / b;
    cout << r; // 4.5

Quick Check

Which university variable fits double best?

  1. tuitionBalance
  2. semesterCount
  3. isFullTime

A. tuitionBalance needs cents, a decimal value.

Code It: Tuition Balance

  • Declare balance
  • Set it to 450.75
  • How would you write it?

    double bal=450.75;

float vs. double

  • float: less precision
  • double: more precision
  • This course uses double

Type: char

  • One single character
  • Wrapped in single quotes
  • e.g., a grade letter

    char grade = 'A';
    char initial = 'S';

Quick Check

Which is a valid char value?

  1. 'A'
  2. "A"
  3. A

A. char uses single quotes, one character.

Quick Check

Which university variable fits char best?

  1. letterGrade
  2. studentID
  3. creditHours

A. letterGrade is one character, like 'A'.

Code It: Letter Grade

  • Declare letterGrade
  • Set it to 'B'
  • How would you write it?

    char letterGrade='B';

Type: bool

  • Only true or false
  • Named after George Boole
  • e.g., isEnrolled, passed

    bool isEnrolled=true;
    bool passed = false;

bool in Practice

  • Stores yes/no answers
  • Used a lot in decisions
  • if (isEnrolled) later on

    bool ok=grade>=60;
    cout << ok; // 1

Quick Check

Which university variable fits bool best?

  1. isEnrolled
  2. major
  3. unitsTaken

A. isEnrolled is only ever true or false.

Code It: Is Enrolled

  • Declare isEnrolled
  • Set it to true
  • How would you write it?

    bool isEnrolled=true;

Type: string

  • Text: words, sentences
  • Wrapped in double quotes
  • Needs #include <string>

    #include <string>
    string name="Alice";

What Is +=?

  • Shorthand for reassignment
  • x += 5 means x = x + 5
  • Also -=, *=, /=, %=

    int x = 10;
    x += 5; // x = x + 5
    // x is now 15

Compound Assignment Ops

  • += add and assign
  • -= subtract and assign
  • *=, /=, %= work the same

    int credits = 12;
    credits += 3; // 15
    credits -= 2; // 13

Quick Check

What does x += 5; do?

  1. Sets x to 5
  2. Sets x to x + 5
  3. Compares x to 5

B. x += 5; reassigns x to x + 5.

Code It: Running Total

  • Declare total = 0 (int)
  • Add 10 using +=
  • Print total
  • How would you write it?

    int total = 0;
    total += 10;
    cout << total;

Code It: Countdown Seats

  • Declare seats = 5 (int)
  • Subtract 1 using -=
  • Print seats
  • How would you write it?

    int seats = 5;
    seats -= 1;
    cout << seats;

string in Practice

  • Store any length of text
  • Can combine with +
  • e.g., building a message

    string first = "Ana";
    string last = "Lee";
    string full = first;
    full += " ";
    full += last;

Quick Check

Which university variable fits string best?

  1. studentName
  2. birthYear
  3. isGraduate

A. studentName holds text, a person's name.

Code It: Student Name

  • Declare studentName
  • Set it to "Maria"
  • How would you write it?

    string studentName =
        "Maria";

Quick Check

Which type would you use for a course name?

  1. int
  2. bool
  3. string

C. string stores text like a course name.

Naming Rules

  • Start with a letter or _
  • No spaces, no dashes
  • Case-sensitive: age ≠ Age

    int age;   // valid
    int _temp; // valid
    int 2fast; // invalid

Naming Conventions

  • Use descriptive names
  • camelCase in C++
  • Not just x, y, z

    int studentCount;
    int sc;

Case Styles in C++

  • camelCase: variables
  • PascalCase: class names
  • ALL_CAPS: constants

    int studentAge;
    class Student {};
    const int MAX_A=100;

Choosing Good Names

  • Be specific, not generic
  • Avoid cryptic short names
  • Loop counters (i, j) OK

    int d; // unclear
    int daysLeft;

Quick Check

Which naming style fits a class name?

  1. camelCase
  2. PascalCase
  3. ALL_CAPS

B. PascalCase: Capitalize each word, e.g. Student.

Quick Check

Which variable name is invalid in C++?

  1. studentAge
  2. _temp
  3. 2ndTry

C. Names can't start with a digit.

Code It: A Clearer Name

  • Rename a bad variable: d
  • Make it clear and descriptive
  • How would you write it?

    int daysLeft;

Why Comment Code?

  • Explains why, not just what
  • Helps future you and others
  • Ignored by the compiler

    // A student's GPA
    double gpa = 3.8;

Single-Line Comments

  • Starts with //
  • Runs to end of line
  • Best for short notes

    int credits = 15;

Multi-Line Comments

  • Starts /* ends */
  • Spans several lines
  • Good for longer notes

    /* Explains the grade
       calc below */

Quick Check

Which starts a single-line comment?

  1. //
  2. /* */
  3. #

A. // starts a comment to end of line.

Code It: Add a Comment

  • credits = 15
  • Add a note: units
  • How would you write it?

    // units
    int credits = 15;

Multiple Variables, One Line

  • Same type, comma-separated
  • Each still needs a value
  • Saves a little typing

    int hw1=10, hw2=8;

Swapping Two Variables

  • a = 5, b = 9
  • Need a 3rd, temp variable
  • How would you swap them?

    int a = 5, b = 9;
    int temp = a;
    a = b;
    b = temp;
    // now a=9, b=5

Word Origin: "Constant"

  • Latin: constare, stand firm
  • const means never reassigned
  • Compiler enforces this

Constants: const

  • A variable that can't change
  • Set once, at initialization
  • Protects a fixed value

    const double PI=3.14;
    // PI = 3; // error!

Quick Check

What does the const keyword do?

  1. Deletes the variable
  2. Prevents reassignment
  3. Makes it a string

B. const locks the value after initialization.

Code It: Lock a Constant

  • Declare MAX, an int
  • Lock it at 30, never changes
  • How would you write it?

    const int MAX = 30;

Basic I/O with Types

Where I/O Comes From & Goes To

  • Your code sits in the middle
  • Green in, blue out
  • 4 places data can flow

cout: Printing a Value

  • cout prints to the screen
  • << is the insertion operator
  • endl ends the current line
#include <iostream>

std::cout << pages;
std::cout << std::endl;

cout: Printing a Value

#include <iostream>

std::cout << pages;
std::cout << std::endl;

cin: Reading a Value

  • cin reads keyboard input
  • >> is the extraction operator
  • The value fills a variable
#include <iostream>

std::cin >> pages;

cin: Reading a Value

#include <iostream>

std::cin >> pages;

endl vs. \n

  • Both end the current line
  • endl also flushes the buffer
  • \n is usually a bit faster
#include <iostream>

std::cout << pages;
std::cout << std::endl;
std::cout << pages << "\n";

endl vs. \n

#include <iostream>

std::cout << pages;
std::cout << std::endl;
std::cout << pages << "\n";

The Output Buffer

  • Program doesn't wait on I/O
  • Output waits in a buffer
  • endl flushes it now
  • \n leaves it buffered

Chaining Several Reads

  • One cin can read many values
  • >> again for the next variable
  • We'll reuse this all module
#include <iostream>

std::cin >> pages >> copies;

Chaining Several Reads

#include <iostream>

std::cin >> pages >> copies;

History of Data Types

A Short History of Types

  • 1957: FORTRAN adds named data
  • 1958: ALGOL adds typed vars
  • Every language kept the idea

What Is a Data Type?

  • Sets the box's size & shape
  • Decides what values fit inside
  • int, float, char, bool...

Why Do We Need Types?

  • Fits data in the right size
  • Only legal operations allowed
  • Bugs are caught before running

Why the Printer Needs Types

  • Pages in a job: a whole number
  • Cost per page: needs cents
  • Printer busy: yes or no

The Native C++ Types

  • Seven built-in kinds of data
  • Each has its own size & range
  • Pick the type that fits

Type Ranges & Examples

TypeExampleMinMaxComment
intint pages;-2,147,483,6482,147,483,647Most common whole number
shortshort copiesRequested;-32,76832,767Smaller range, saves memory
longlong printerSerial;-2,147,483,648 or less2,147,483,647 or moreFor very large whole numbers
floatfloat toner = 85.5f;±3.4×1038~7 digits preciseDecimal, needs f suffix
doubledouble costPerPage = 0.08;±1.8×10308~15 digits preciseDecimal, default precision
charchar size = 'L';-128127One character or small number
boolbool busy = true;falsetrueOnly two values

⚠️ long is only guaranteed to match int's range; many systems (Linux/Mac) give it far more.

Today: Programming a Printer

  • You now know all seven types
  • Time to put them to work
  • Every example: a real printer

const: A Value That Can't Change

  • const locks the value in place
  • Reassigning it is an error
  • Good for a fixed max copies
const int MAX_COPIES = 5;
// MAX_COPIES = 8;  // error

const: A Value That Can't Change

const int MAX_COPIES = 5;
// MAX_COPIES = 8;  // error

const Fits: MAX_COPIES

  • A fixed rule, set once
  • Never changes at runtime
  • Perfect for const

const Doesn't Fit: pagesLeft

  • Drops as pages print
  • Needs reassignment each time
  • const would cause an error

  • Use const so it can't change

Whole Numbers

int: The Default Choice

  • Whole numbers, no decimals
  • 4 bytes on most systems
  • The safe default choice
#include <iostream>

int pages;
std::cin >> pages;
std::cout << pages;
std::cout << std::endl;

int: The Default Choice

#include <iostream>

int pages;
std::cin >> pages;
std::cout << pages;
std::cout << std::endl;

int: Fits or Not?

Fits

  • 45
  • -12
  • 1000

 

Does Not Fit

  • 3.14 (a decimal)
  • "A4" (that's text)
  • 'A' (that's a char)

short & long: Other Sizes

  • short: smaller range, less RAM
  • long: bigger range than int
  • Pick based on the value range
#include <iostream>

short copiesRequested;
std::cin >> copiesRequested;
long printerSerial;
std::cin >> printerSerial;

short & long: Other Sizes

#include <iostream>

short copiesRequested;
std::cin >> copiesRequested;
long printerSerial;
std::cin >> printerSerial;

short & long: Fits or Not?

Fits

  • short: 100
  • long: 5000000000

 

Does Not Fit

  • short: 90000 (too big)
  • long: 3.14 (a decimal)

unsigned: Only Positive

  • No negative values allowed
  • Doubles the positive range
  • Great fit for counts
#include <iostream>

unsigned int jobsQueued;
std::cin >> jobsQueued;

unsigned: Only Positive

#include <iostream>

unsigned int jobsQueued;
std::cin >> jobsQueued;

unsigned: Fits or Not?

Fits

  • 0
  • 100
  • 4000000

 

Does Not Fit

  • -5 (negative)
  • 3.14 (a decimal)

sizeof: How Big Is It?

  • sizeof returns bytes used
  • int is usually 4 bytes
  • Sizes can vary by system
#include <iostream>

std::cout << sizeof(int);
// prints 4 on most systems

sizeof: How Big Is It?

#include <iostream>

std::cout << sizeof(int);
// prints 4 on most systems

Real Numbers: float & double

float vs. double: Precision

  • Both store decimal values
  • double: 8 bytes, more precise
  • float: 4 bytes, less precise

float & double: Fits or Not?

Fits

  • 0.08
  • 92.5
  • 3.14159

 

Does Not Fit

  • "high" (that's text)
  • true (that's a bool)

Why Precision Matters

  • Printing costs need accuracy
  • double avoids rounding drift
  • Printer uses double for cost
double costPerPage = 0.08;
double totalCost = 12.40;

Why Precision Matters

double costPerPage = 0.08;
double totalCost = 12.40;

The f Suffix

  • float literals need an f
  • Without it, it's a double
  • Mixing types can surprise you
float toner = 85.5f;
double costPerPage = 0.08;
// 0.08 alone is a double

The f Suffix

float toner = 85.5f;
double costPerPage = 0.08;
// 0.08 alone is a double

Integer Division Gotcha

  • int / int drops the decimal
  • 100 / 3 in ints equals 33
  • Use a double to keep it exact
#include <iostream>

int t = 100, j = 3;
std::cout << t / j;
// prints 33, not 33.3
std::cout << t / (double)j;

Integer Division Gotcha

#include <iostream>

int t = 100, j = 3;
std::cout << t / j;
// prints 33, not 33.3
std::cout << t / (double)j;

Assignment & Reassignment

Declaring vs. Initializing

  • Declare: create the empty box
  • Initialize: fill it right away
  • pagesLeft; vs pagesLeft = 5;

How Assignment Works

  • = copies a value into the box
  • The box's old value is gone
  • Right side, then left side

Reassignment: New Value

  • Same variable, new value
  • Printing fewer pages left
  • Only the latest value survives

Uninitialized Variables

What If You Skip Init?

  • int pagesLeft; // no value
  • What's really inside the box?
  • It's not always zero!

Local Variables: Garbage Values

  • Declared inside a function
  • Memory isn't cleared first
  • The value is unpredictable
#include <iostream>

int pagesLeft;
std::cout << pagesLeft;
// prints garbage, not 0

Local Variables: Garbage Values

#include <iostream>

int pagesLeft;
std::cout << pagesLeft;
// prints garbage, not 0

Global & static: Zero by Default

  • Declared outside any function
  • C++ zero-initializes these
  • Safe, but easy to forget why
int totalPagesPrinted;
// starts at 0
// only true globally

Global & static: Zero by Default

int totalPagesPrinted;
// starts at 0
// only true globally

Default Values by Type

TypeLocal (auto)Global/static
intgarbage0
doublegarbage0.0
chargarbage'\0'
boolgarbagefalse

Practice: Spot the Bug

  • This local int has no value
  • What does this actually print?
  • Why is that risky?
#include <iostream>

int pagesLeft;
std::cout << pagesLeft;
std::cout << std::endl;
// what prints here?

Why This Matters

  • Uninitialized data misleads
  • Always give data a real value
  • A habit that prevents bugs

Bits & Bytes

The Bit & The Byte

  • 1948: word "bit" coined
  • 1964: IBM sets 8-bit byte
  • Every type sized in bytes

What Is a Bit? What Is a Byte?

Bits Per Native Type

TypeBytesBitsRange
bool18true or false only
char18-128 to 127
short216-32K to 32K
int432-2.1B to 2.1B
long4 or 8*32 or 64*at least -2.1B to 2.1B
float432±3.4×1038
double864±1.8×10308

⚠️ long's size varies by system: 4 bytes on Windows, 8 on Linux/Mac.

The ASCII Table

CategoryDecimal RangeExample
Control chars0 – 3110 = newline
Space, punctuation32 – 4732 = space
Digits 0–948 – 5748 = '0'
More punctuation58 – 6463 = '?'
Uppercase A–Z65 – 9065 = 'A'
More punctuation91 – 9695 = '_'
Lowercase a–z97 – 12297 = 'a'

⚠️ ASCII only covers 0–127; wider text needs Unicode.

From Character to Bits

  • char stores 1 byte
  • 'A' is ASCII 65
  • 65 in binary: 01000001

If/Else Statements

  • Branching: pick a path
  • Every language has it
  • C++ inherited it from C

Where If/Else Shows Up

What Is a Condition?

if / else Syntax

  • Condition goes in ( )
  • Braces group each block
  • else needs no condition
  • else runs only if false
if (condition) {
    // runs when true
}
else {
    // runs when false
}

True or False?

int age = 20;
if (age >= 18)
TRUE

True or False?

int credits = 9;
if (credits > 12)
FALSE

True or False?

char grade = 'B';
if (grade == 'A')
FALSE

True or False?

double gpa = 3.5;
if (gpa >= 3.5)
TRUE

True or False?

bool passed = true;
if (passed)
TRUE

True or False?

int absences = 0;
if (absences != 0)
FALSE

True or False?

int score = 59;
if (score < 60)
TRUE

True or False?

bool enrolled = false;
if (enrolled)
FALSE

Combining Conditions

OpMeaningExample
&&both must be truea && b
||either can be truea || b
!flips true/false!a

⚠️ && needs both true; a single false fails it.

Branches

Agenda

  1. What Is a Branch?
  2. Decision-Making
  3. Real-World Examples

  6. Practice Lab
  7. Practice Lab Part 2

What Is a Branch?

What Is a Branch?

  • Programs need to make choices
  • A branch picks one path
  • Example: check the paper tray
bool paperTrayFull = true;
if (paperTrayFull) {
    cout << "Ready to print";
}

What Is a Branch?

  • Each branch runs on its own
  • Only one path executes
  • Example: printer online?
bool printerOnline = false;
if (printerOnline) {
    cout << "Sending job...";
} else {
    cout << "Printer offline!";
}

What Is a Branch?

  • A condition is true or false
  • Never both at once
  • Example: is toner available?
bool tonerOk = true;
if (tonerOk) {
    cout << "Printing...";
} else {
    cout << "Refill toner";
}

Word Origin: "Boolean"

George Boole
  • English mathematician, 1800s
  • Self-taught, no formal degree
His 1854 Book
  • "An Investigation of the
  • Laws of Thought"
  • Logic expressed as algebra

Boole showed that true/false logic could be written as math – AND, OR, NOT. C++'s bool type is named after him directly.

Questions?

Decision-Making

Decision-Making in Programs

  • Check if the printer is jammed
  • Avoids damage and wasted pages
bool printerJam = true;
if (printerJam) {
    cout << "Clear the jam";
} else {
    cout << "Printer ready";
}

Decision-Making in Programs

  • Compare tray to the job
  • Picks the matching tray
int tray = 1;
if (tray == 1) {
    cout << "Tray 1 selected";
} else if (tray == 2) {
    cout << "Tray 2 selected";
} else {
    cout << "Invalid tray";
}

Decision-Making in Programs

  • Check toner and paper both
  • Required before a batch job
bool paper = true;
bool toner = false;
if (paper && toner) {
    cout << "Starting batch";
} else {
    cout << "Check supplies";
}

Real-World Examples

Card Swipe Door

  • Check if the card is valid
  • Grant or deny access
#include <iostream>
bool cardValid = false;
if (cardValid) {
    cout << "Door opens";
} else {
    cout << "Access denied";
}

Extend: Card Swipe Door

  • Add a maintenance check
  • Locked doors deny entry
#include <iostream>
bool maintenance = false;
if (maintenance) {
    cout << "Door locked";
} else if (cardValid) {
    cout << "Door opens";
} else {
    cout << "Access denied";
}

Traffic Light

  • Check the light color
  • Decide: go, slow, or stop
#include <iostream>
char light = 'Y';
if (light == 'G') {
    cout << "Go";
} else if (light == 'Y') {
    cout << "Slow down";
} else {
    cout << "Stop";
}

Extend: Traffic Light

  • Add a broken-light case
  • Trace light = 'X'
#include <iostream>
// light = 'X'
if (light == 'G') {
    cout << "Go";
} else if (light == 'Y') {
    cout << "Slow down";
} else if (light == 'X') {
    cout << "Light broken";
} else {
    cout << "Stop";
}

ATM Machine

  • Check if the PIN is correct
  • Grant or deny access
#include <iostream>
bool pinCorrect = false;
if (pinCorrect) {
    cout << "Access granted";
} else {
    cout << "Incorrect PIN";
}

Extend: ATM Machine

  • Add a 3-attempt limit
  • Block the card at 3
#include <iostream>
int attempts = 3;
if (attempts >= 3) {
    cout << "Card blocked";
} else if (pinCorrect) {
    cout << "Access granted";
} else {
    cout << "Incorrect PIN";
}

Elevator

  • Compare requested to current
  • Picks a direction to move
#include <iostream>
int requested = 5, current = 3;
if (requested > current) {
    cout << "Going up";
} else if (requested < current) {
    cout << "Going down";
} else {
    cout << "Already there";
}

Extend: Elevator

  • Add an overweight check
  • Overweight blocks moving
#include <iostream>
bool overweight = true;
if (overweight) {
    cout << "Overweight, exit";
} else if (requested > current) {
    cout << "Going up";
} else {
    cout << "Going down";
}

Smart Thermostat

  • Check the current temperature
  • Turn heating or cooling on
#include <iostream>
int temp = 68;
if (temp < 70) {
    cout << "Heating ON";
} else if (temp > 75) {
    cout << "Cooling ON";
} else {
    cout << "System idle";
}

Extend: Smart Thermostat

  • Add a system-off state
  • Off skips heat/cool
#include <iostream>
bool systemOn = false;
if (!systemOn) {
    cout << "System OFF";
} else if (temp < 70) {
    cout << "Heating ON";
} else {
    cout << "Cooling ON / idle";
}

Coffee Machine

  • Check water and bean levels
  • Brew only if both are ready
#include <iostream>
bool water = true, beans = false;
if (water && beans) {
    cout << "Brewing...";
} else {
    cout << "Refill first";
}

Extend: Coffee Machine

  • Add a cup-present check
  • No cup blocks brewing
#include <iostream>
bool cupPresent = false;
if (!cupPresent) {
    cout << "Insert a cup";
} else if (water && beans) {
    cout << "Brewing...";
} else {
    cout << "Refill first";
}

Password Login

  • Track which attempt this is
  • Lock out after 3 tries
#include <iostream>
int attempt = 1;
if (attempt == 1) {
    cout << "Wrong, try again";
} else if (attempt == 2) {
    cout << "Wrong, last try";
} else if (attempt == 3) {
    cout << "Account locked";
}

Extend: Password Login

  • Add an already-locked check
  • Block any further tries
#include <iostream>
bool locked = true;
if (locked) {
    cout << "Account is locked";
} else if (attempt < 3) {
    cout << "Wrong, try again";
} else {
    cout << "Account locked";
}

if / else in C++

If / Else Statements

  • Basic conditional check
  • Two possible paths only
  • if(cond) {...} else {...}
#include <iostream>
int temp = 75;
if (temp > 70) {
    cout << "Turn on AC";
} else {
    cout << "AC off";
}

Else If

  • Handles several conditions
  • First true one runs
  • Good for priority checks
#include <iostream>
int score = 82;
if (score >= 90) {
    cout << "A";
} else if (score >= 75) {
    cout << "B";
} else {
    cout << "C or below";
}

Best Practices

  • Keep conditions readable
  • Use braces every time
  • Avoid deep nesting
#include <iostream>
if (isReady) {
    cout << "Ready";
} else {
    cout << "Not ready";
}

Common Mistakes

  • Using = instead of ==
  • Forgetting the else case
#include <iostream>
bool active = true;
if (active = false) {  // bug
    cout << "Inactive";
}

Common Mistakes

  • Loose condition checked first
  • Stricter case never runs
#include <iostream>
int score = 85;
if (score >= 60) {
    cout << "Pass"; // bug: catches 85
} else if (score >= 80) {
    cout << "Honors";
}

⚠️ Put the stricter condition first, or the looser one always wins.

Common Mistakes

  • Missing braces on if
  • Only next line is inside if
#include <iostream>
bool ready = false;
if (ready)
    cout << "Go";
    cout << "Oops, always runs";

Quick Check

  • Good for many discrete values?
#include <iostream>
int mode = 2;
if (mode == 1) {
    cout << "B&W";
} else if (mode == 2) {
    cout << "Color";
}

Answer: No, prefer switch for many discrete values.

Nested If

  • Checks conditions inside
  • another if block
  • Reduce nesting when you can
#include <iostream>
if (hasPaper) {
    if (tonerOk) {
        cout << "Ready";
    }
} else {
    cout << "Add paper";
}

Logical Operators

  • && needs both true
  • || needs just one true
#include <iostream>
bool paper = true;
bool toner = true;
if (paper && toner) {
    cout << "Printing...";
}

Short-Circuit Evaluation

  • Checked left to right
  • Stops once outcome is known
#include <iostream>
if (isConnected && hasJob) {
    cout << "Processing";
}

Summary: If / Else

  • Use for two-way choices
  • Keep it short and readable
#include <iostream>
bool ready = true;
if (ready) {
    cout << "Go";
} else {
    cout << "Wait";
}

Questions?

switch in C++

Advantages of if/else

  • Any condition, any type
  • Works with ranges (>, <)
  • Combine with &&, ||

Where switch Helps

  • Many else-if gets messy
  • Hard to read one value
  • switch reads cleaner here

⚠️ Many options on one value? switch reads cleaner.

Switch Statement

  • Alternative to many else-if
  • Works on int, char, enum
#include <iostream>
int mode = 2;
switch(mode) {
    case 1: cout << "B&W"; break;
    case 2: cout << "Color"; break;
    default: cout << "Unknown";
}

Best Practices

  • Always break each case
  • Add a default case
#include <iostream>
char opt = 'B';
switch(opt) {
    case 'A': cout << "Opt A"; break;
    case 'B': cout << "Opt B"; break;
    default: cout << "Invalid";
}

Multiple Cases, One Action

  • Stack cases to group them
  • Avoids repeating code
#include <iostream>
char grade = 'B';
switch(grade) {
    case 'A':
    case 'B': cout << "Pass"; break;
    default: cout << "Fail";
}

Switch With Enum

  • Enums improve readability
#include <iostream>
enum Mode { BW=1, COLOR=2 };
Mode m = COLOR;
switch(m) {
    case BW: cout << "B&W"; break;
    case COLOR: cout << "Color"; break;
}

Quick Check

  • switch or if/else for 4 modes?
#include <iostream>
int mode = 3;
switch(mode) {
    case 1: cout << "B&W"; break;
    case 2: cout << "Color"; break;
    case 3: cout << "Draft"; break;
}

Answer: switch, it's more readable for discrete values.

Fallthrough Cases

  • Omitting break runs the
  • next case too, on purpose
#include <iostream>
char c = 'A';
switch(c) {
    case 'A':
    case 'B': cout << "Good"; break;
    case 'C': cout << "Average";
}

Default Case

  • Catches unexpected values
  • Prevents silent bugs
#include <iostream>
int opt = 5;
switch(opt) {
    case 1: cout << "One"; break;
    default: cout << "Unknown";
}

Quick Check

  • What if you forget break?
#include <iostream>
int x = 2;
switch(x) {
    case 1: cout << "One";
    case 2: cout << "Two"; // falls
    case 3: cout << "Three";
}

Answer: Execution falls through to the next case.

Summary: Switch

  • Best for discrete values
  • Always add default
#include <iostream>
char opt = 'C';
switch(opt) {
    case 'C': cout << "Option C"; break;
    default: cout << "Unknown";
}

Traffic Light

  • Check the light color
  • One case per color
#include <iostream>
char light = 'G';
switch (light) {
    case 'G': cout << "Go"; break;
    case 'Y': cout << "Slow down"; break;
    default: cout << "Stop";
}

Elevator Floor Button

  • Pick the floor to visit
  • One case per floor
#include <iostream>
int floor = 3;
switch (floor) {
    case 1: cout << "Lobby"; break;
    case 2: cout << "Office"; break;
    case 3: cout << "Gym"; break;
    default: cout << "Invalid floor";
}

Vending Machine

  • Pick a snack by number
  • One case per snack
#include <iostream>
int choice = 2;
switch (choice) {
    case 1: cout << "Chips"; break;
    case 2: cout << "Candy"; break;
    case 3: cout << "Soda"; break;
    default: cout << "Sold out";
}

ATM Menu

  • Pick an action by number
  • One case per menu item
#include <iostream>
int choice = 1;
switch (choice) {
    case 1: cout << "Withdraw"; break;
    case 2: cout << "Deposit"; break;
    case 3: cout << "Balance"; break;
    default: cout << "Invalid choice";
}

Word Origin: "Switch"

Electrical Roots
  • A physical lever that
  • picks one circuit path
In Code
  • Same idea: pick ONE case
  • based on a value

The metaphor is literal: an old telephone switchboard physically routed a call down one wire, exactly one path, out of many.

Practice Lab

Requirements

  • Build a text Horse Race Game
  • Track: Start, Middle, Finish
  • Player picks Move or Quit
  • Print the horse's position
// Goal:
// Start -> Middle -> Finish
// Two player choices get there

Step 1: Track the Position

  • Use constants, not magic
  • numbers, for each spot
const int START = 0;
const int MIDDLE = 1;
const int FINISH = 2;
int horsePos = START;

Step 2: Ask for a Move

  • 1 = Move Forward, 2 = Quit
  • Store the answer in choice
int choice;
cout << "1=Move, 2=Quit: ";
cin >> choice;

Step 3: Handle the Choice

  • if/else moves the horse
  • or ends the game
if (choice == 1) {
    horsePos = MIDDLE;
    cout << "Horse: _ H _";
} else {
    cout << "You quit.";
    return 0;
}

Step 4: Second Move

  • Ask again, this time
  • using switch instead
switch(choice) {
    case 1:
        horsePos = FINISH;
        cout << "Horse: _ _ H";
        break;
    case 2:
        cout << "You quit.";
        break;
}

Step 5: Check the Winner

  • Compare position to FINISH
  • Print a win message
if (horsePos == FINISH) {
    cout << "You won!";
}

Deliverables

  • A working horse_race.cpp
  • Uses if/else AND switch
  • Handles both Quit points
// Submit horse_race.cpp
// Test: choose Move, Move
// Test: choose Quit at step 1

Problem 1: Campus Coffee

  • Coffee is $4 a cup
  • Student ID: $1 off a cup
  • Read how many cups
  • No if, no loop yet
Cups: 3
You pay: $9

Answer 1: Campus Coffee

  • Two consts: price, deal
  • Subtract once for the deal
  • Multiply by the cups
int cups;
const int PRICE = 4;
const int DEAL = 1;
std::cout << "Cups: ";
std::cin >> cups;
int each = PRICE - DEAL;
std::cout << "You pay: $" << cups * each;

Problem 2: Coffee Size

  • 1 small, 2 medium, 3 large
  • Prices: $3, $4, $5
  • Read the size number
  • Use if / else if
Size (1-3): 2
Price: $4

Answer 2: Coffee Size

  • One branch per size
  • else if checks the next
  • Last else covers large
int size;
std::cout << "Size (1-3): ";
std::cin >> size;
if (size == 1) std::cout << "Price: $3";
else if (size == 2) std::cout << "Price: $4";
else std::cout << "Price: $5";

Before Problem 3: while

  • while (test) { body }
  • Runs while the test is true
  • Body must move toward false
  • Else it loops forever

⚠️ If the body never changes the test, the loop runs forever.

Problem 3: Seat Numbers

  • Read a count n (an int)
  • Print 1, 2, 3, up to n
  • One number per line
  • Use a while loop

Answer 3: Seat Numbers

  • seat starts at 1
  • Loop while seat is not past n
  • seat = seat + 1 each pass
int n;
std::cout << "How many seats? ";
std::cin >> n;
int seat = 1;
while (seat <= n) {
    std::cout << seat << std::endl;
    seat = seat + 1;
}

Problem 4: Sum to Sentinel

  • Read scores, one per line
  • Stop when the user types -1
  • Add each score to a total
  • Print the total at the end
Score: 8
Score: 9
Score: 7
Score: -1
Total: 24

Answer 4: Sum to Sentinel

  • Read once before the loop
  • Loop until the score is -1
  • Read again inside the loop
int total = 0;
int score;
std::cout << "Score: ";
std::cin >> score;
while (score != -1) {
    total = total + score;
    std::cout << "Score: ";
    std::cin >> score;
}
std::cout << "Total: " << total;

Problem 5: Validate Units

  • Units must be 1 to 18
  • Re-ask while out of range
  • Accept the first valid one
  • Then print "Registered"
Units: 25
Range 1-18. Units: 0
Range 1-18. Units: 15
Registered: 15

Answer 5: Validate Units

  • The test is the bad case
  • || means either side is off
  • Re-read until the test fails
int units;
std::cout << "Units: ";
std::cin >> units;
while (units < 1 || units > 18) {
    std::cout << "Range 1-18. Units: ";
    std::cin >> units;
}
std::cout << "Registered: " << units;

Problem 6: Coffee Card

  • Card needs 10 stamps
  • Each coffee is one stamp
  • Loop while stamps under 10
  • Write the pseudocode

Answer 6: Coffee Card

  • Start stamps at 0
  • Test before the body
  • Stops at exactly 10
set stamps = 0
while stamps < 10
    buy one coffee

print "free coffee unlocked"

Bonus Game: Rock Paper Scissors

  • 1 rock, 2 paper, 3 scissors
  • You type your move
  • Computer picks with rand()
  • if decides win, lose, or tie

Step 1: The Libraries

  • cstdlib gives rand / srand
  • ctime gives time
  • srand seeds it once
  • Seed with the clock so it
  • differs each run
#include <cstdlib>   // rand(), srand()
#include <ctime>     // time()

srand(time(0));   // seed from the clock
int you, cpu, n = 1;

Step 2: Pick Moves Each Round

  • while runs 3 rounds
  • Read your move into you
  • rand() % 3 gives 0, 1, 2
  • + 1 shifts it to 1, 2, 3
while (n <= 3) {
    std::cout << "You (1-3)? ";
    std::cin >> you;
    cpu = rand() % 3 + 1;   // 0,1,2 -> 1,2,3
    // decide the winner (next slide)
    n = n + 1;
}

Step 3: Decide the Winner

  • Same number is a tie
  • you % 3 + 1 is the move
  • that beats you
  • Anything else, you win
if (you == cpu)
    std::cout << "Tie\n";
else if (you % 3 + 1 == cpu)
    std::cout << "You lose\n";
else
    std::cout << "You win\n";

Sample Run

  • Rock vs scissors: win
  • Paper vs scissors: lose
  • Rock vs rock: tie
You (1-3)? 1
You win
You (1-3)? 2
You lose
You (1-3)? 1
Tie

Module 4

Loops

Agenda

  1. What Is a Loop?
  2. The while Loop
  3. The for Loop
  4. The do-while Loop
  5. Nested Loops
  6. break, continue, Pitfalls
  7. Practice Lab
  8. Practice Lab Part 2

What Is a Loop?

  • Repeat a block of code
  • A test decides when to stop
  • C++: while, for, do-while

Loops Beat Copy-Paste

  • Print 1 to 100 by hand?
  • One loop does it all
  • Fix it once, not 100 times

The Three Parts of a Loop

  • Start: set a counter
  • Test: keep going?
  • Update: step the counter

Word Origin: "Iteration"

iter-
  • Latin "iterum": again
iterare
  • Latin verb: to repeat

One iteration is one pass through the loop body; the word just means doing it again.

Questions?

The while Loop

The while Loop

  • Check the test first
  • Then run the body
  • Body must move the test
int x = 1;
while (x <= 5) {
    std::cout << x << " ";
    x = x + 1;
}
// prints: 1 2 3 4 5

while: Trace the Count

  • x starts at 1
  • Loop while x <= 5
  • x goes up each pass

while: Read Until a Sentinel

  • Read one value first
  • Loop until it is -1
  • Add each to a total
int total = 0;
int num;
std::cin >> num;
while (num != -1) {
    total = total + num;
    std::cin >> num;
}
std::cout << "sum = " << total;

while: Avoid the Infinite Loop

  • No update means never stop
  • Always change the test
  • Ctrl+C stops a runaway
// BAD: x never changes
int x = 1;
while (x <= 3) {
    std::cout << x;   // 1 1 1 ...
}
// FIX: add  x = x + 1;  in the body

Questions?

The for Loop

The for Loop

  • All three parts, one line
  • Best when the count is known
  • init, then test, then body
for (int i = 1; i <= 5; i++) {
    std::cout << i << " ";
}
// prints: 1 2 3 4 5

for Equals while

  • for is a packed while
  • Same init, test, update
  • Pick the clearer one

for: Add 1 to n

  • Read n from the user
  • Loop i from 1 to n
  • sum = sum + i
int n, sum = 0;
std::cin >> n;
for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) {
    sum = sum + i;
}
std::cout << "sum = " << sum;

Questions?

The do-while Loop

The do-while Loop

  • Body runs first
  • Test is at the bottom
  • Always runs at least once
int choice;
do {
    std::cout << "1=Play 2=Quit: ";
    std::cin >> choice;
} while (choice != 2);
std::cout << "Bye!";

do-while vs while

  • while: may run 0 times
  • do-while: runs 1+ times
  • Menus fit do-while

Questions?

Nested Loops

Nested Loops

  • A loop inside a loop
  • Inner runs fully each pass
  • Good for grids and tables
for (int r = 1; r <= 3; r++) {
    for (int c = 1; c <= 3; c++) {
        std::cout << "(" << r << c << ")";
    }
    std::cout << "\n";
}

Nested: Trace the Grid

  • Outer picks the row
  • Inner sweeps the columns
  • 3 x 3 is 9 passes

Nested: Draw a Chessboard

  • 8 by 8 nested loop
  • (row + col) % 2 picks color
  • No array needed
for (int r = 0; r < 8; r++) {
    for (int c = 0; c < 8; c++) {
        if ((r + c) % 2 == 0)
            std::cout << "W ";
        else
            std::cout << "B ";
    }
    std::cout << "\n";
}

Questions?

break, continue, Pitfalls

break and continue

  • break: leave the loop now
  • continue: skip to next pass
  • Use them sparingly
for (int i = 1; i <= 5; i++) {
    if (i == 3) continue;  // skip 3
    if (i == 5) break;     // stop
    std::cout << i << " ";
}
// prints: 1 2 4

Off-by-One Errors

  • 0 to <= 5 runs 6 times
  • 0 to < 5 runs 5 times
  • Count the passes on paper
// runs 6 times: 0 1 2 3 4 5
for (int i = 0; i <= 5; i++)
    std::cout << i;

// runs 5 times: 0 1 2 3 4
for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++)
    std::cout << i;

Loop Pitfalls Checklist

  • Did the test change?
  • Right start and end?
  • One job per loop

From Rounds to Randomness

  • Start simple: fixed rounds
  • Then add real randomness
  • Same loops, new games

Countdown Game

  • Goal: reach zero and stop
  • Counts down from n to 1
  • One line per number
  • Then a final message
int n = 5;
for (int i = n; i >= 1; i--) {
    std::cout << i << "\n";
}
std::cout << "Blast off!\n";

Lucky Number Game

  • Goal: find 7 in fewest tries
  • Target is fixed: 7
  • Loop while wrong guess
  • Counts the tries
int lucky = 7, guess = 0, tries = 0;
while (guess != lucky) {
    std::cin >> guess;
    tries++;
}
std::cout << "Tries: " << tries;

Lucky Number: Trace It

  • 3 is too low
  • 5 is too low
  • 7 matches, loop stops

What Is rand()?

  • Returns a random int
  • Range: 0 to RAND_MAX
  • Needs #include <cstdlib>

Picking a Range with %

  • % keeps the remainder
  • rand() % 6 gives 0-5
  • +1 shifts it to 1-6

Adding Randomness: rand()

  • rand() gives a random int
  • % picks a range
  • srand seeds it once
#include <cstdlib>
#include <ctime>
srand(time(0));  // seed once
int roll = rand() % 6 + 1;
// roll is 1 to 6

Why Seed with time(0)?

  • No seed: same numbers
  • time(0) changes each run
  • Seed once, at the top
// BAD: same random numbers every run
int roll = rand() % 6 + 1;

// FIX: seed once with time(0)
srand(time(0));
int roll = rand() % 6 + 1;

Rolling One Die

  • 6 equally likely faces
  • rand() % 6 + 1 picks one
  • Same odds every time

Dice Roll Game

  • Goal: simulate n dice rolls
  • Roll n times in a loop
  • Each roll: rand() % 6 + 1
  • Print every roll
srand(time(0));
for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) {
    int roll = rand() % 6 + 1;
    std::cout << i << ": " << roll << "\n";
}

Dice Roll: Sample Output

  • Four rolls, one per line
  • Numbers come from rand()
  • Your run will differ

Guess the Random Number

  • Goal: guess the hidden number
  • Target: rand() % 100 + 1
  • do-while: guess once first
  • Loop until correct
srand(time(0));
int target = rand() % 100 + 1;
int guess, tries = 0;
do {
    std::cin >> guess;
    tries++;
} while (guess != target);

Win Streak Game

  • Goal: land 3 heads in a row
  • Simulates repeated coin flips
  • Any tails resets the streak
  • No fixed round limit
srand(time(0));
int streak = 0;
while (streak < 3) {
    int flip = rand() % 2;
    if (flip == 1) streak++;
    else streak = 0;
}
std::cout << "Got 3 heads!\n";

Stone, Scissors, Paper

  • Goal: win the most rounds
  • 0=stone 1=scissors 2=paper
  • Best of 5 rounds
srand(time(0));
int wins = 0;
for (int i = 1; i <= 5; i++) {
    int cpu = rand() % 3;  // pick 0,1,2
    // if/else decides the winner
    // wins++ when you beat cpu
}
std::cout << "Wins: " << wins;

Games Recap: Loop Choices

  • Known count: use for
  • Unknown count: use while
  • Guess at least once: do-while

  • Declare an int n
  • Prompt the user
  • Read it with cin
int n;
std::cout << "Number: ";
std::cin >> n;

Step 2: Loop 1 to 10

  • A for loop, i from 1
  • Runs while i <= 10
  • i++ each pass
for (int i = 1; i <= 10; i++) {
    // print this row
}

Step 3: Print n times i

  • Build the row text
  • n, then i, then n * i
  • End each with "\n"

    std::cout << n << " x " << i;
    std::cout << " = " << n * i << "\n";
}

Password Attempts

  • Goal: unlock in 3 tries
  • PIN is fixed, tries limited
  • while loop, checks tries left
  • Stops early if correct
const int PIN = 4821;
int guess, tries = 0;
bool ok = false;
while (tries < 3 && !ok) {
    std::cin >> guess;
    tries++;
    ok = (guess == PIN);
}
if (ok) std::cout << "Access OK\n";
else std::cout << "Locked out\n";

Math Quiz

  • Goal: answer 5 math problems
  • for loop, fixed 5 rounds
  • Random a + b each round
  • Tally correct answers
srand(time(0));
int score = 0;
for (int i = 1; i <= 5; i++) {
    int a = rand() % 10 + 1;
    int b = rand() % 10 + 1;
    int ans;
    std::cin >> ans;
    if (ans == a + b) score++;
}
std::cout << "Score: " << score;

Why Arrays? The Problem

The Problem: Too Many Names

  • The Registrar tracks 200 GPAs
  • One variable per student?
  • That's 200 variable names

Individual Variables Don't Scale

  • 30 grades need 30 variables
  • Adding student 31? New line
  • Looping over them? Impossible

⚠️ A fixed number of variables can never loop over an unknown number of students.

Existing Software Solves This

  • Spreadsheets: one column
  • Databases: one table
  • Same idea, different tool

Word Origin: "Array"

arayer
  • Old French: to set in order
arrangier
  • To arrange, line up in a row

An array is values lined up in order, each one numbered by position.

The Answer: One Array

  • One name: grades
  • Five values, side by side
  • Each has its own position

Declaring & Indexing

Declaring an Array

  • Type, name, size in brackets
  • Creates empty slots
  • Fill each slot by index
int grades[5];
// 5 empty int slots
grades[0] = 92;
grades[1] = 78;

Zero-Based Counting

  • Indexing starts at 0
  • Not 1, like counting people
  • Last index is size - 1

⚠️ The first slot is index 0, not index 1.

Word Origin: "Index"

index
  • Latin: pointer, one who shows
indicare
  • To point out, indicate

An index literally points to one slot in the array.

Reading an Element

  • Reading an element
  • Use the index in brackets
  • grades[0] is the first grade
std::cout << grades[0];
// prints 92
std::cout << grades[4];
// prints 67, the last one

Updating an Element

  • Writing updates a slot
  • Old value is overwritten
  • Same syntax as reading
grades[2] = 95;
// updates slot 2
std::cout << grades[2];
// now prints 95

Initializing All at Once

  • List values at declare time
  • No index-by-index filling
  • Great for known starting data
int seats[3] = {40, 35, 28};
// fill all 3 at once
std::cout << seats[1];
// prints 35

Practice: What Prints?

  • seats[0] = 40, seats[1] = 35
  • cout << seats[1];
  • What is printed?

Answer: 35

Looping Through Arrays

Why Loop an Array?

  • for loop visits every index
  • i goes from 0 to size - 1
  • grades[i] changes each pass

Printing Every Grade

  • i < 5 stops at index 4
  • i++ moves to the next slot
  • Prints every grade, one line
for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
    std::cout << grades[i] << "\n";
}

Sum All Grades

  • total starts at 0
  • Add each grade in the loop
  • The Registrar needs this sum
int total = 0;
for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
    total += grades[i];
}
std::cout << total;

Average All Grades

  • Average = total ÷ count
  • Use 5.0, not 5, for the count
  • Int division would truncate
double avg = total / 5.0;
// 5.0, not 5: avoid int division
std::cout << avg;

⚠️ total / 5 (int / int) drops the decimal part entirely.

Find the Highest Grade

  • Start by assuming slot 0 wins
  • Compare every later slot
  • Keep the biggest one seen
int highest = grades[0];
for (int i = 1; i < 5; i++) {
    if (grades[i] > highest) {
        highest = grades[i];
    }
}

Find the Lowest Grade

  • Same pattern, flipped operator
  • Start at slot 0, scan the rest
  • Keep the smallest one seen
int lowest = grades[0];
for (int i = 1; i < 5; i++) {
    if (grades[i] < lowest) {
        lowest = grades[i];
    }
}

Count Passing Grades

  • Loop + condition + array
  • Count grades 70 or above
  • Records reports pass rates
int passing = 0;
for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
    if (grades[i] >= 70) {
        passing++;
    }
}

Practice: Trace the Loop

  • grades = {92, 78, 85, 100, 67}
  • Count grades >= 90
  • How many pass?

Answer: 2 (92 and 100)

Array Bugs to Avoid

Arrays Have a Fixed Size

  • Size is fixed at declaration
  • int grades[5] is always 5
  • No 6th slot ever appears

Bug: Off-by-One

  • <= 5 checks index 5 too
  • Index 5 doesn't exist!
  • Valid indexes are 0 to 4
for (int i = 0; i <= 5; i++) {
    std::cout << grades[i];
}

⚠️ <= instead of < reads one slot past the array's end.

Bug: Out-of-Bounds

  • Out-of-bounds isn't caught
  • C++ doesn't stop you
  • Result: garbage or a crash

🚨 Reading past the end is undefined behavior, not a clean error.

Practice: Spot the Bug

  • int nums[3];
  • for (int i = 0; i <= 3; i++)
  • What's wrong here?

Answer: <= 3 reads index 3, which doesn't exist

The Fix: Match Size Exactly

  • Match the loop bound to size
  • size() (vectors) helps later
  • Never hardcode a guess
int names[30];
// or grades, or any array
for (int i = 0; i < 30; i++)

Vectors: Growing Arrays

Why Vectors?

  • A new student enrolls today
  • Arrays can't grow to fit them
  • We need a resizable container

Word Origin: "Vector"

vehere
  • Latin: to carry, to convey
C++ STL, 1998
  • A container that can grow

A vector "carries" a sequence of values and can grow as needed.

Declaring a Vector

  • Needs #include <vector>
  • std::vector<type> name
  • Starts with zero elements
#include <vector>
std::vector<int> grades;
// starts empty, size 0

Adding a New Student

  • push_back adds to the end
  • The vector grows automatically
  • New student? Just push_back
grades.push_back(92);
grades.push_back(78);
// size is now 2

Vector Size: .size()

  • Replaces guessing the size
  • Always accurate, never guessed
  • Use it as the loop bound
std::cout << grades.size();
// how many elements right now

Looping a Vector

  • Same [ ] indexing as arrays
  • Loop bound is grades.size()
  • Works no matter the count
for (int i = 0; i < grades.size(); i++) {
    std::cout << grades[i] << "\n";
}

This loop never needs a manual off-by-one fix. size() always matches.

Arrays vs. Vectors

  • Know the exact count? Array
  • Runtime count? Use a vector
  • Both use [ ] to read/write

2D Arrays: Tables

A Grade Table

  • A table: rows and columns
  • Every student, every grade
  • One array of arrays

Declaring a 2D Array

  • Two sizes: rows, then columns
  • table[row][col] finds a cell
  • Each cell is one grade
int table[2][2];
// 2 students, 2 assignments
table[0][0] = 92;
// Dana, HW1

Looping a 2D Array

  • Outer loop: each row
  • Inner loop: each column
  • Nested loops, from Module 4
for (int r = 0; r < 2; r++) {
    for (int c = 0; c < 2; c++) {
        std::cout << table[r][c] << " ";
    }
    std::cout << "\n";
}

Practice: Print the Table

  • table[0][0]=92, table[0][1]=88
  • table[1][0]=78, table[1][1]=81
  • What does row 1 print?

Answer: 78 81

Real Software Uses 2D Too

  • Spreadsheets store data too
  • Image pixels: row and column
  • Same 2D-array idea underneath

Recap: Arrays & Vectors

  • Array: fixed, fast, simple
  • Vector: grows, more flexible
  • 2D array: a grid of values

Questions?

Practice Lab

Dice Roll Tally

  • Roll a die, store every result
  • Count how often each face hits
  • Find the most common roll

Requirements

  • Ask the class for N (rolls)
  • Store each roll in an array
  • Count each face 1 through 6

Step 1: Declare the Rolls Array

  • rolls holds up to 20 values
  • n is the actual roll count
  • 20 is just a safe upper limit
int n; // ask the class
int rolls[20];
// up to 20 rolls

Step 2: Roll and Store

  • Loop n times, once per roll
  • rand() % 6 + 1 gives 1 to 6
  • Store it directly in the array
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    rolls[i] = rand() % 6 + 1;
}

Uses the same rand() from Module 4. Still needs srand(time(0)) once, at the top of main.

Step 3: Print All Rolls

  • Loop through every stored roll
  • One line, space-separated
  • Confirms the array filled
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    std::cout << rolls[i] << ' ';
}

Step 4: A Tally Array

  • tally[0] counts face 1
  • tally[5] counts face 6
  • Every counter starts at zero
int tally[6] = {0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0};
// one counter per face

⚠️ Use tally[roll - 1], not tally[roll]. Face 1 lives at index 0.

Step 5: Count with a Condition

  • All three ideas at once
  • if checks the roll is valid
  • roll-1 maps face to index
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    if (rolls[i] >= 1 && rolls[i] <= 6) {
        tally[rolls[i] - 1]++;
    }
}

Step 6: Print the Tally

  • f+1 turns index into a face
  • Prints face, then its count
  • One line per face, 1 through 6
for (int f = 0; f < 6; f++) {
    std::cout << (f+1);
    std::cout << ": " << tally[f] << "\n";
}

Step 7: Find the Most Common Roll

  • Same find-the-max pattern
  • best tracks the top index
  • best + 1 is the winning face
int best = 0;
for (int f = 1; f < 6; f++) {
    if (tally[f] > tally[best]) {
        best = f;
    }
}

Sample Output

  • n = 20 rolls, six tallies
  • Face 3 and face 6 tie at 5
  • Code keeps the first max seen

Deliverable

  • Write it: roll, tally, print
  • Show output for n = 20
  • One line: which face won, why

Questions?

Practice Lab Part 2

A Real System to Build

  • Not a game: a real system
  • A host seats real guests
  • No table gets double-booked

Existing Software Solves This

  • OpenTable, Resy: real apps
  • Same core idea underneath
  • We'll build a small version

Requirements

  • Track every table: free or not
  • Take reservations one by one
  • Stop when the floor is full

Warm-Up: One Row of Tables

  • Start small: just one row
  • 10 tables, numbered 0 to 9
  • Scale up once this works

Plan Your Variables

  • One int per table: 0 or 1
  • 0 means empty, 1 means taken
  • int, not bool: matches later

Step 1: Declare the Row

  • row holds 10 table slots
  • Index 0 is the 1st table
  • Not yet given a value
int row[10];  // 10 tables

Step 2: Fill It with Zeros

  • Loop once per table
  • 0 means the table is free
  • Runs before anyone arrives
for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) {
    row[i] = 0;
}

Step 3: Print the Row

  • Loop through every table
  • Print each status in order
  • Confirms the row is empty
for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) {
    std::cout << row[i] << ' ';
}

Check: What Does It Print?

  • After Steps 1-2-3 run
  • row has 10 tables, all free
  • What appears on screen?

Answer: What Does It Print?

// ten zeros, space-separated
// one 0 per table, all free

One Row Isn't Enough

  • A real floor has many rows
  • One array can't hold a grid
  • Need rows AND columns

⚠️ A 1D array can't hold a grid: it has no row and column.

Ten Rows of Ten

  • 10 rows, 10 tables each
  • 100 tables total on the floor
  • Row and column find each one

Plan Your Variables: The Floor

  • Same 0/1 idea, one more index
  • tables[row][col] finds one
  • row and col each 0 through 9

Step 4: Declare the Floor

  • 10 rows, 10 tables per row
  • Two sizes: [rows][columns]
  • All 100 still unset
int tables[10][10];

⚠️ Row comes first, then column: tables[row][col].

Step 5: Empty Every Table

  • Outer loop: pick the row
  • Inner loop: pick the column
  • Every cell starts at 0
for (int r = 0; r < 10; r++) {
  for (int c = 0; c < 10; c++) {
    tables[r][c] = 0;
  }
}

Step 6: Print the Floor

  • Inner loop prints one row
  • \n starts the next row
  • Result: a 10x10 grid on screen
for (int r = 0; r < 10; r++) {
  for (int c = 0; c < 10; c++) {
    std::cout << tables[r][c];
  }
  std::cout << "\\n";
}

Check: Rows or Columns First?

  • tables[2][7]: row 2, col 7
  • Which loop must be OUTER?
  • So each full row prints first

Answer: Rows or Columns First?

// outer = row: r = 2
// inner = col: c = 0..9
// tables[2][7] is the 8th
// cell printed on row 2

Requirements: One Reservation

  • Ask which table: row, column
  • Check the number is valid
  • Reserve it, or say it is taken

Step 7: Ask for a Table

  • Two ints: row and column
  • One cin reads both at once
  • Host types them, space apart
int r, c;
std::cin >> r >> c;

Step 8: Check the Table Number

  • Row and column: 0 through 9
  • Anything else is off the floor
  • Catch it before using it
if (r < 0 || r > 9 ||
    c < 0 || c > 9) {
  std::cout << "No such table";
}

Step 9: Is It Empty?

  • 0 means nobody has it yet
  • Runs before we reserve it
  • Guards against double-booking
if (tables[r][c] == 0) {
  // reserve it: Step 10
}

Step 10: Reserve It

  • 1 marks the table as taken
  • Only runs inside the if above
  • Confirms it back to the host
tables[r][c] = 1;
std::cout << "Reserved!";

Step 11: Already Taken

  • else runs when it was not free
  • Same row/col, no change made
  • Host tries a different table
else {
  std::cout << "Table taken";
}

Sample Run: One Reservation

  • Host asked for table 2, 7
  • It was free, now reserved
  • Grid shows a 1 at row 2, col 7

How Do We Know We're Full?

  • Count every table still at 0
  • Zero empty means fully booked
  • Recheck after each reservation

Step 12: Count Empty Tables

  • Same nested loop as Step 5
  • empty grows by 1 each 0 found
  • Reruns after every booking
int empty = 0;
for (int r = 0; r < 10; r++)
 for (int c = 0; c < 10; c++)
  if (tables[r][c] == 0) empty++;

Step 13: The Reservation Loop

  • while keeps going as long
  • as empty is above zero
  • Body: Steps 7 through 11
while (empty > 0) {
  // Steps 7-11 go here
}

Step 14: Recount After Each Booking

  • Last line inside the while
  • Rerun Step 12 to update empty
  • Loop rechecks the new value
while (empty > 0) {
  // ask, check, reserve
  // then recount:
  empty = 0;
  // (Step 12 loop again)
}

Step 15: Fully Booked

  • Loop ends on its own
  • empty reached zero
  • One message after the loop
// after the while loop ends:
std::cout << "Fully booked!";

Check: Trace the Loop

  • 99 tables reserved, 1 free
  • That 1 gets booked next
  • What does empty equal then?

Answer: Trace the Loop

// before: empty == 1
// reserve the last table
// recount: empty == 0
// while (0 > 0) is false
// loop stops, prints message

Sample Run: Filling the Floor

  • Booking after booking
  • Grid fills with 1s over time
  • Stops the moment empty hits 0

Beyond Booking

  • Same array, more features
  • Cancel, count, search, report
  • Each is a small new loop

Extension 1: Cancel a Reservation

  • Ask for a taken table
  • Set it back to 0: free again
  • empty grows by 1
tables[r][c] = 0;
empty++;
std::cout << "Canceled";

Extension 2: Count Reservations So Far

  • 100 minus empty tables
  • No new loop needed
  • One line, using what we track
int reserved = 100 - empty;

Extension 3: Occupancy Percentage

  • reserved out of 100 tables
  • 100.0 keeps the math decimal
  • Prints like "42.0%"
double pct = reserved * 100.0 / 100;
std::cout << pct << '%';

Extension 4: Find the First Empty Table

  • Same nested loop shape again
  • Stops at the first 0 it finds
  • Suggests a table to the host
for (int r = 0; r < 10; r++)
 for (int c = 0; c < 10; c++)
  if (tables[r][c] == 0) {
    // first empty: r, c
  }

Extension 5: Reprompt on Invalid Input

  • while re-asks until it fits
  • Loops back to Step 7 & 8
  • Host can never enter table 15
while (r < 0 || r > 9) {
  std::cout << "Try again: ";
  std::cin >> r;
}

Extension 6: Print Only Reserved Tables

  • Same grid scan, one more if
  • Skips every table still at 0
  • Shorter than the full grid
for (int r = 0; r < 10; r++)
 for (int c = 0; c < 10; c++)
  if (tables[r][c] == 1)
   std::cout << r << c << '\n';

Check: Extension Trace

  • Table (4, 4) just canceled
  • It was the only taken table
  • What does occupancy % show?

Answer: Extension Trace

// reserved = 100 - empty
// empty becomes 100 again
// reserved = 0
// pct = 0.0  (0% occupied)

Reading tables[row][col]

  • First [ ]: which row
  • Second [ ]: which column
  • Order never swaps, ever

The Whole Program: Structure

  • Setup: declare & empty floor
  • Loop: ask, check, book, count
  • After: fully booked message

Recap: What We Used

  • A 1D array, then a 2D array
  • Nested loops: row, then column
  • if/else and a while loop
  • cin for input, cout for output

Deliverable

  • Build the reservation system
  • Book, cancel, and find a table
  • Show it running fully booked

Questions?

Looking Ahead: Module 6

Where We Are: Module 5

  • Module 5 done: arrays, vectors
  • Next: User-Defined Functions

Module 6

User Defined Functions

Agenda

  1. Why Functions?
  2. Declaring & Calling
  3. Parameters & Returns
  4. void & Prototypes
  5. Scope & Lifetime
  6. Pass by Reference
  7. Overloading & Defaults
  8. Practice Lab
  9. Practice Lab Part 2
  10. Practice Lab Part 3

The Problem: Repeated Code

  • Bill for 3 cars
  • Same formula, pasted 3 times
  • Fix one? Fix all three
double a = 3 * 120.0 + 35.0;
double b = 5 * 120.0 + 35.0;
double c = 2 * 120.0 + 35.0;

Copy-Paste Breaks

  • Shop fee rises to 40
  • Find every pasted copy
  • Miss one: a wrong bill

⚠️ Every pasted copy is a place a bug can hide.

Existing Software Solves This

  • Excel: =SUM(A1:A5)
  • Calculators: a sqrt button
  • Name it once, reuse it

Word Origin: "Function"

functio
  • Latin: a performance
fungi
  • Latin: to perform, carry out

A function is a named task the program can perform on demand.

The Answer: A Named Block

  • Write the formula once
  • Give the block a name
  • Call the name anywhere

Check: Why Not Copy-Paste?

The shop fee rises from 35 to 40. With 3 pasted copies of the formula, how many places must you edit?

Answer
Three, and missing one gives a wrong bill. With one function, you edit one place.

Functions You Already Use

  • main is a function
  • sqrt is a function
  • Both use a name and ( )
#include <cmath>
int main() {
  double r = std::sqrt(81.0);
  std::cout << r;   // 9
  return 0;
}

Check: Spot the Function

In std::sqrt(81.0), which part is the function name, and which part is the input?

Answer
sqrt is the name. 81.0 is the input, passed inside the parentheses.

Questions?

Declaring & Calling

Anatomy of a Function

  • Return type, then the name
  • Parameters go in ( )
  • The body goes in { }

Requirements: Repair Bill

  • Given the labor hours
  • Compute the repair bill
  • Do it for any car

Step 1: Define a Function

  • double: what it gives back
  • cost: the name we chose
  • Body sits between braces
double cost() {
  return 3 * 120.0 + 35.0;
}

Step 2: Call It

  • Write the name and ( )
  • The call runs the body
  • The value comes back
int main() {
  double bill = cost();
  std::cout << bill;
  return 0;
}

Define Before You Call

  • Compiler reads top to bottom
  • cost must appear above main
  • Else: not declared
double cost() {
  return 395.0;
}

int main() {
  std::cout << cost();
}

⚠️ Calling a function before its definition is a compile error.

Check: Above or Below?

main calls cost(). Should cost be written above or below main, and why?

Answer
Above. The compiler reads top to bottom, so it must know cost before the call.

Trace: What Prints?

What does this program print?

int five() { return 5; }

int main() {
  std::cout << five() + 2;
}
Answer
7. five() returns 5, and then 5 + 2 is 7.

Many Calls, One Definition

  • Call cost() as often as needed
  • Its body is written once
  • Each call runs it again

Check: Count the Bodies

cost() is called in three places in main. How many times is its body written?

Answer
Once. Every call reuses that single body.

Recap: Declaring & Calling

  • Define: type name() { }
  • Call: name();
  • Define above the call

Questions?

Parameters & Returns

The Problem: One Fixed Answer

  • cost() always gives 395
  • Cars need other hours
  • We must pass a number in

Word Origin: "Parameter"

para + metron
  • Greek: beside + measure
parametrum
  • Modern Latin, 1600s

A parameter is a measurable value that stands beside the formula.

Parameters vs. Arguments

  • Parameter: the placeholder
  • Argument: the real value
  • In cost(3), 3 is one

Step 1: Add a Parameter

  • int hours: a local variable
  • Each call fills it in
  • Use it inside the body
double cost(int hours) {
  return hours * 120.0 + 35.0;
}

Step 2: Pass an Argument

  • 3 fills in hours
  • 5 fills it the next time
  • One function, many answers
double a = cost(3);
double b = cost(5);
std::cout << a << " " << b;

Check: Which Value?

double cost(int hours) returns hours * 100.0. What does cost(3) return?

Answer
300.0. hours is 3, and 3 * 100.0 is 300.0.

Step 3: Two Parameters

  • Separate them with commas
  • Each needs its own type
  • Calls pass them in order
double cost(int hours, double rate) {
  return hours * rate + 35.0;
}

Order Matters

  • Arguments match by position
  • First goes to hours
  • Swapped: a wrong bill
cost(3, 120.0);   // right
cost(120.0, 3);   // wrong order

⚠️ The compiler may accept swapped arguments of convertible types and still give a wrong answer.

Check: Match the Arguments

double cost(int hours, double rate). In cost(2, 150.0), what is rate?

Answer
150.0. Arguments match parameters by position, so 2 goes to hours.

Return Values

  • return sends a value back
  • Its type matches the function
  • The function ends there

Word Origin: "Return"

retourner
  • Old French: to turn back
return
  • Result turns back to caller

A return hands the result back to the code that made the call.

Using the Returned Value

  • Store it in a variable
  • Or print it directly
  • Or use it in math
double t = cost(3, 120.0);
std::cout << cost(5, 120.0);
double all = t + cost(2, 120.0);

Return Ends the Function

  • Code after return is skipped
  • First return that runs wins
  • Use it to exit early
int half(int n) {
  return n / 2;
  std::cout << "never";  // skipped
}

Check: Write max2

Write max2: it takes two ints and returns the larger one.

int max2(int a, int b) {
  if (a > b) {
    return a;
  }
  return b;
}

Check: Which Return Type?

A function averages two int MPG readings and may give 34.5. Which return type fits, int or double?

Answer
double. An int would drop the .5, so 34.5 would become 34.

Example: MPG Rating

  • Takes an mpg, returns a char
  • Several returns, one runs
  • Reads like a rating scale
char rating(int mpg) {
  if (mpg >= 40) return 'A';
  if (mpg >= 30) return 'B';
  if (mpg >= 20) return 'C';
  if (mpg >= 10) return 'D';
  return 'F';
}

Check: Trace rating(35)

Using rating() from the last slide, what does rating(35) return?

Answer
'B'. 35 fails the >= 40 test, then passes >= 30, so it returns 'B'.

Recap: Parameters & Returns

  • Parameters take input
  • return sends output
  • Types must match

Questions?

void & Prototypes

Functions With No Result

  • Some functions just do work
  • Print a header, log a line
  • No value comes back

Word Origin: "Void"

voide
  • Old French: empty
vacivus
  • Latin: empty, unoccupied

A void function returns nothing: its result slot is empty.

Step 1: A void Function

  • void: nothing comes back
  • No return value needed
  • It just prints a banner
void banner() {
  std::cout << "== AutoCare ==\n";
}

Step 2: Call a void Function

  • Call it as its own statement
  • No variable to store into
  • Cannot be used in math
int main() {
  banner();
  std::cout << "Oil Change\n";
  banner();
}

Check: void or Not?

Which one needs a return type other than void: printReceipt() or totalFee()?

Answer
totalFee. It hands a number back. printReceipt only prints, so it is void.

The Ordering Problem

  • main is often written first
  • Helpers sit below it
  • The compiler wants a heads-up

Word Origin: "Prototype"

protos
  • Greek: first
typos
  • Greek: impression, model

A prototype is the first, early model of a function: just its shape.

Step 3: Write a Prototype

  • Signature only, then a ;
  • Goes above main
  • The body can live below
double cost(int hours);   // prototype

int main() {
  std::cout << cost(3);
}

double cost(int hours) {
  return hours * 120.0;
}

Check: Will This Build?

The prototype says double cost(int). The definition says double cost(double). Will it build?

Answer
No. They are different functions, so the prototype has no body and linking fails.

Questions?

Scope & Lifetime

Where Is a Variable Seen?

  • A variable lives in its braces
  • Outside them it is unknown
  • Each function has its own

Word Origin: "Scope"

skopos
  • Greek: a target, a watcher
scopo
  • Italian: aim, purpose

Scope is the range a variable can see: its field of view.

Local Variables

  • total exists only in cost
  • main cannot read it
  • It vanishes on return
double cost(int hours) {
  double total = hours * 120.0;
  return total;
}
// total is unknown out here

Error: Out of Scope

  • cost(3) ran and finished
  • Its total is already gone
  • main cannot see total
int main() {
  cost(3);
  std::cout << total;   // error
}

⚠️ A local variable is destroyed when its function returns.

Check: Can main See It?

cost declares double total inside its braces. Can main print total? Why?

Answer
No. total is local to cost. main only gets its value if cost returns it.

Same Name, No Clash

  • twice changes its own n
  • main's n stays 5
  • Each call gets a fresh n
int twice(int n) {
  n = n * 2;
  return n;
}
// main: int n = 5; twice(n);
// main's n is still 5

Trace: Which n?

What does this program print?

int twice(int n) { return n * 2; }

int main() {
  int n = 4;
  twice(n);
  std::cout << n;
}
Answer
4. twice returned 8, but the result was thrown away and main's n never changed.

Global vs. Parameter

  • const globals are safe
  • The value never changes
  • A name beats a magic 35
const double SHOP_FEE = 35.0;

double bill(int hours) {
  return hours * 120.0 + SHOP_FEE;
}

Check: Global or Param?

hours changes for every car. Should it be a global variable or a parameter?

Answer
A parameter. Data that changes belongs in a parameter, not in a global.

Recap: Scope & Lifetime

  • Locals live in their braces
  • They die on return
  • Same name, separate boxes

Questions?

Pass by Reference

Copies by Default

  • Arguments are copied in
  • The function edits the copy
  • Your variable stays the same

Pass by Value

  • bump changes only n
  • x is untouched
  • This is pass by value
void bump(int n) {
  n = n + 10;
}
// main: int x = 5;
// bump(x);  x is still 5

Trace: Did x Change?

What does this program print?

void bump(int n) { n = n + 10; }

int main() {
  int x = 5;
  bump(x);
  std::cout << x;
}
Answer
5. bump changed its own copy of x, not x itself.

Word Origin: "Reference"

referre
  • Latin: to carry back
reference
  • A name for the original

A reference is a second name that carries you back to the same variable.

Pass by Reference

  • Add & after the type
  • No copy: a second name
  • Edits change the original

Step 1: Add the &

  • int& means a reference
  • n is x itself
  • The body is unchanged
void bump(int& n) {
  n = n + 10;
}

Step 2: Call It

  • The call looks the same
  • x becomes 15
  • No copy was made
int x = 5;
bump(x);
std::cout << x;   // 15

Check: Spot the Difference

One character separates pass by value from pass by reference in the parameter list. Which one?

Answer
The &. int& n is a reference to the original; int n is a copy.

Example: Swap Two Values

  • Both parameters are references
  • A temp holds one value
  • Swaps the callers' variables
void swap2(int& a, int& b) {
  int tmp = a;
  a = b;
  b = tmp;
}

Trace: After the Swap

Using swap2 from the last slide, what prints?

int x = 3;
int y = 8;
swap2(x, y);
std::cout << x << " " << y;
Answer
8 3. Both parameters are references, so x and y themselves were swapped.

Arrays as Parameters

  • Arrays are never copied
  • It edits the real one
  • Pass the size too
void zero(int a[], int n) {
  for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)
    a[i] = 0;
}
// zero(readings, 5);

Check: Why Pass n?

Why must zero() take n as a second parameter?

Answer
An array parameter does not carry its length. The function needs n to know where to stop.

Recap: Pass by Reference

  • Value: a copy is edited
  • Reference: the original
  • Arrays: always the original

Questions?

Overloading & Defaults

Same Name, Different Inputs

  • C++ allows one name twice
  • Parameter lists must differ
  • The compiler picks a match

Overloading cost()

  • Two versions of cost
  • Different parameter lists
  • Both are valid together
double cost(int hours) {
  return hours * 120.0;
}
double cost(int hours, double rate) {
  return hours * rate;
}

Check: Which cost() Runs?

Given the two cost() versions, which one runs for cost(3), and which for cost(3, 150.0)?

Answer
cost(3) runs the one-parameter version. cost(3, 150.0) runs the two-parameter one.

Default Arguments

  • rate has a default value
  • The caller may leave it out
  • cost(3) uses 120.0
double cost(int hours,
           double rate = 120.0) {
  return hours * rate;
}

Check: Which Rate?

With the default above, what rate does cost(3) use? What about cost(3, 150.0)?

Answer
cost(3) uses 120.0. cost(3, 150.0) uses 1600.0: a passed argument overrides the default.

Defaults Go Last

  • Right-most parameters only
  • No gaps allowed
  • Else: a compile error

⚠️ A parameter with a default cannot come before one without.

Check: Is It Legal?

Is double cost(double rate = 120.0, int hours) legal C++?

Answer
No. Once a parameter has a default, every parameter after it needs one too.

Questions?

Practice Lab

Requirements: Service Shop Tool

  • Compute a repair bill
  • Turn an MPG into a rating
  • Report the average MPG

Plan Your Functions

Name the three functions this tool needs, and the return type of each.

Answer
cost: double. rating: char. average: double. Each takes the input it needs.

Step 1: Prototypes

  • Signatures go above main
  • Bodies come below main
  • The tool reads top-down
double cost(int hours);
char rating(int mpg);
double average(int g[], int n);

Step 2: cost()

  • Hours times the rate
  • Plus a flat 35.0 shop cost
  • Returns the bill
double cost(int hours) {
  return hours * 120.0 + 35.0;
}

Step 3: rating()

  • Highest cutoff first
  • Returns as soon as one hits
  • F is the fallback
char rating(int mpg) {
  if (mpg >= 40) return 'A';
  if (mpg >= 30) return 'B';
  if (mpg >= 20) return 'C';
  return 'F';
}

Step 4: average()

  • Loop over n readings
  • Add each into sum
  • Divide by n at the end
double average(int g[], int n) {
  double sum = 0;
  for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)
    sum += g[i];
  return sum / n;
}

Check: Why i < n?

In average(), why does the loop stop at i < n and not at a fixed 5?

Answer
The array does not know its length. Using n lets one function work for any fleet size.

Step 5: Ask the Class

  • Read the hours taken
  • Ask the class for a value
  • Store it in an int
int hours;
std::cout << "Hours: ";
std::cin >> hours;   // ask the class

Step 6: MPG Report

  • Five MPGs in an array
  • rating() per reading
  • average() for the fleet
int g[5] = {42, 28, 35, 51, 18};
for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++)
  std::cout << rating(g[i]) << " ";
std::cout << average(g, 5);

Sample Run: Service Shop Tool

  • Hours from the class
  • MPGs come from the array
  • Every result via a function

Extension: void Helper

Write a void function printLine that prints a line of 20 dashes.

void printLine() {
  std::cout << "--------------------\n";
}

Extension: By Reference

Write refuel(double& tank) that adds 5.0 to the caller's tank.

void refuel(double& tank) {
  tank = tank + 5.0;
}
// refuel(t);  t changes

Deliverable

  • Write all three functions
  • Add printLine and refuel
  • Run it, show the output
