Practice Lab Part 2

Minesweeper: The Game

  • A grid hides some mines
  • Reveal a cell: safe or boom
  • Numbers count nearby mines

The Rules

  • Click a cell to reveal it
  • A mine ends the game
  • A number: mines touching it

Win or Lose

  • Reveal a mine: you lose
  • Reveal all safe cells: you win
  • Numbers guide safe guesses

Plan Your Functions

  • Break the game into pieces
  • Each piece: one function
  • Functions call each other

Why Functions First?

  • Each function: one clear job
  • Loops and arrays live inside
  • main() calls them in order

Step 1: Board Constants

  • SIZE: the board is 6x6
  • A named constant, not 6
  • Used everywhere below
const int SIZE = 6;

Step 2: Declare the Arrays

  • board: {LT}0{GT} mines, count
  • revealed: has this cell shown?
  • Both sized SIZE x SIZE
int board[SIZE][SIZE];
bool revealed[SIZE][SIZE];

Step 3: Function Prototypes

  • Declared above main()
  • Bodies come after main()
  • One line per function
void initBoard(int b[SIZE][SIZE]);
void placeMines(int b[SIZE][SIZE], int n);
int countAdjacent(int b[SIZE][SIZE],
                  int r, int c);
void fillNumbers(int b[SIZE][SIZE]);

Check: Why Prototypes?

  • main() calls initBoard()
  • Its body is below main()
  • What goes wrong without one?
// Without a prototype, the
// compiler has not seen
// initBoard yet: build error.

Requirements: initBoard

  • Takes the board array
  • Every cell starts at 0
  • Runs once, before anything

Step 4: initBoard, the Loop

  • Outer loop: pick the row
  • Inner loop: pick the column
  • Nested: every cell, once
void initBoard(int b[SIZE][SIZE]) {
  for (int r = 0; r < SIZE; r++) {
    for (int c = 0; c < SIZE; c++) {
      // fill this cell next
    }
  }
}

Step 5: initBoard, Fill It

  • b[r][c]: this exact cell
  • 0 means no mine, no count
  • Same shape, every cell
void initBoard(int b[SIZE][SIZE]) {
  for (int r = 0; r < SIZE; r++)
    for (int c = 0; c < SIZE; c++)
      b[r][c] = 0;
}

Check: How Many Cells Set?

  • SIZE is 6
  • The nested loop runs fully
  • How many cells get set to 0?
// 6 rows times 6 columns
// = 36 cells, each set once

Requirements: placeMines

  • Takes the board and mine count
  • Picks random empty cells
  • Marks each as a mine: -1

Step 6: placeMines, Seed First

  • srand: makes rand() vary
  • time(0): a different seed
  • Call this once, in main()
// in main(), before placing:
srand(time(0));

Step 7: placeMines, the Loop

  • placed: mines so far
  • Loop while placed < n
  • Stops once n mines are down
void placeMines(int b[SIZE][SIZE], int n) {
  int placed = 0;
  while (placed < n) {
    // pick a cell next
  }
}

Step 8: placeMines, Pick a Cell

  • rand() % SIZE: 0 through 5
  • One call for row, one for col
  • A random spot each time
int r = rand() % SIZE;
int c = rand() % SIZE;

Step 9: placeMines, Avoid Repeats

  • -1 already means a mine
  • Skip it: try again next loop
  • Otherwise: place the mine
if (b[r][c] == -1) {
  continue;
}
b[r][c] = -1;
placed++;

⚠️ Skipping a used cell is what stops two mines landing in one spot.

Check: What Does -1 Mean?

  • A cell can be 0, 1-8, or -1
  • placeMines just set one to -1
  • What does that cell now hold?
// -1 marks a mine.
// 0-8 will later mean:
// mines touching that cell.

The 8 Neighbors

  • Center cell: (1,1)
  • Check all 8 cells around it
  • Skip the center itself

Requirements: countAdjacent

  • Takes the board, one row, col
  • Checks the 8 cells around it
  • Returns how many are mines

Step 10: countAdjacent, Setup

  • count: mines found so far
  • dr, dc range -1 to 1
  • That pair covers all 8 cells
int countAdjacent(int b[SIZE][SIZE],
                  int r, int c) {
  int count = 0;
  for (int dr = -1; dr <= 1; dr++) {
    // inner loop next
  }
  return count;
}

Step 11: countAdjacent, Inner Loop

  • dc also -1 to 1
  • nr, nc: the neighbor's spot
  • r+dr, c+dc: one of the 8
for (int dc = -1; dc <= 1; dc++) {
  int nr = r + dr, nc = c + dc;
  // check nr, nc next
}

Step 12: countAdjacent, Skip Self

  • dr==0 and dc==0: that's (r,c)
  • Not a neighbor of itself
  • continue: skip this pair
if (dr == 0 && dc == 0) {
  continue;
}

Step 13: countAdjacent, Bounds Check

  • A neighbor may be off-grid
  • nr, nc must stay 0..SIZE-1
  • Off the grid: skip it too
if (nr < 0 || nr >= SIZE ||
    nc < 0 || nc >= SIZE) {
  continue;
}

⚠️ Skipping the bounds check crashes on edge and corner cells.

Step 14: countAdjacent, Tally It

  • b[nr][nc] == -1: a mine there
  • Found one: count goes up
  • After both loops: return count
if (b[nr][nc] == -1) {
  count++;
}

Check: Trace a Corner Cell

  • (0,0) has only 3 neighbors
  • The other 5 pairs go off-grid
  • How many pairs get skipped?
// 5 of the 8 (dr, dc) pairs
// point off the grid and get
// skipped by the bounds check.

Requirements: fillNumbers

  • Runs after mines are placed
  • Every safe cell gets its count
  • Calls countAdjacent for each

Step 15: fillNumbers

  • Skip cells that are already -1
  • Otherwise: call countAdjacent
  • Store the result in that cell
void fillNumbers(int b[SIZE][SIZE]) {
  for (int r = 0; r < SIZE; r++)
    for (int c = 0; c < SIZE; c++)
      if (b[r][c] != -1)
        b[r][c] = countAdjacent(b, r, c);
}

Check: Does Order Matter?

  • fillNumbers reads other cells
  • Must mines be placed first?
  • What if fillNumbers ran first?
// Yes: fillNumbers counts
// existing -1 mines. Run it
// too early: every count is 0.

Requirements: printBoard

  • Shows hidden cells as #
  • Shows revealed cells: number
  • Never shows an unrevealed mine

Step 16: printBoard, the Loop

  • Same nested-loop shape again
  • One character printed per cell
  • A newline after each row
void printBoard(int b[SIZE][SIZE],
                bool rv[SIZE][SIZE]) {
  for (int r = 0; r < SIZE; r++) {
    for (int c = 0; c < SIZE; c++) {
      // print one cell next
    }
    std::cout << "\\n";
  }
}

Step 17: printBoard, Hidden Cells

  • rv[r][c] false: not revealed
  • Print a # instead of the value
  • Keeps mines a secret
if (!rv[r][c]) {
  std::cout << '#';
}

Step 18: printBoard, Revealed Cells

  • rv[r][c] true: show the value
  • A 0 still prints as 0
  • A safe count like 3 too
else {
  std::cout << b[r][c];
}

Check: What Prints First Turn?

  • No cell is revealed yet
  • rv is all false at the start
  • What does printBoard show?
// A full 6x6 grid of #,
// since every rv[r][c]
// still equals false.

Requirements: revealCell

  • Marks one cell as revealed
  • Returns true if it was a mine
  • main() reacts to that result

Step 19: revealCell

  • bool return: true means mine
  • Set revealed first, always
  • Then check what was under it
bool revealCell(int b[SIZE][SIZE],
                bool rv[SIZE][SIZE],
                int r, int c) {
  rv[r][c] = true;
  return b[r][c] == -1;
}

Check: True or False?

  • b[2][2] holds a 3
  • You call revealCell(b,rv,2,2)
  • What does it return?
// false: b[2][2] is 3,
// not -1, so it is not a
// mine. The cell is revealed.

Requirements: isWon

  • Checks every non-mine cell
  • All revealed: the game is won
  • One hidden safe cell: not won

Step 20: isWon

  • Look for one hidden safe cell
  • Found one: return false
  • None found: the player won
bool isWon(int b[SIZE][SIZE],
            bool rv[SIZE][SIZE]) {
  for (int r = 0; r < SIZE; r++)
    for (int c = 0; c < SIZE; c++)
      if (b[r][c] != -1 && !rv[r][c])
        return false;
  return true;
}

Check: One Cell Left

  • Every safe cell is revealed
  • Except one, still hidden
  • What does isWon return?
// false: that one hidden,
// non-mine cell makes the
// loop return false right away.

Requirements: main()

  • Set up the board once
  • Loop: show board, ask, reveal
  • Stop on a mine or a win

Step 21: main(), Setup

  • Seed random, then set up
  • Order: mines placed, then fill
  • Ten mines on a 6x6 board
srand(time(0));
initBoard(board);
placeMines(board, 6);
fillNumbers(board);

Step 22: main(), the Game Loop

  • won starts false
  • Loop while not won
  • Body: print, ask, reveal
bool won = false;
while (!won) {
  printBoard(board, revealed);
  // ask for a cell next
}

Step 23: main(), Ask for a Cell

  • Two ints: row and column
  • One cin reads both
  • Player types them, space apart
int r, c;
std::cout << "Row col: ";
std::cin >> r >> c;

Step 24: main(), Reveal It

  • hitMine: true if it was one
  • revealCell does the real work
  • Next: react to hitMine
bool hitMine = revealCell(board,
                            revealed, r, c);

Step 25: main(), Lose Path

  • hitMine true: game over
  • Print the board one last time
  • break: exit the while loop
if (hitMine) {
  printBoard(board, revealed);
  std::cout << "Boom! You lost.";
  break;
}

Step 26: main(), Win Path

  • isWon: checks the whole board
  • True: set won, loop will stop
  • False: while loop runs again
won = isWon(board, revealed);
if (won) {
  printBoard(board, revealed);
  std::cout << "You win!";
}

Sample Run: A Few Turns

  • Board reprints after each move
  • A number: safe, keep going
  • Boom or You win: the loop ends

Check: Trace the Break

  • revealCell returns true
  • main() checks hitMine next
  • What happens right after that?
// The board prints once more,
// a lose message shows, and
// break exits the while loop.

How It All Fits Together

  • main() calls each function
  • Setup runs once, loop repeats
  • Every piece has one clear job

Recap: What We Used

  • Functions: one job each
  • Nested loops: rows and columns
  • Arrays: the board and revealed
  • if/else: bounds, mine checks

Extension 1: Flag a Cell

  • A flagged array, like revealed
  • Player marks a suspected mine
  • printBoard shows F, not #
bool flagged[SIZE][SIZE];
// set true on a flag command
// printBoard checks it before #

Extension 2: Count Remaining

  • Track safe cells still hidden
  • Total safe cells, minus shown
  • Print it each turn as a hint
['int total = SIZE * SIZE - 6;', '// subtract revealed count too']

Extension 3: Bigger Board

  • Change SIZE to a larger value
  • Scale the mine count with it
  • Everything else stays the same
['const int SIZE = 10;', 'placeMines(board, 15);']

Deliverable

  • Write all seven functions
  • Add one extension you like
  • Play it: win once, lose once

Practice Lab Part 3

CampusNav: The Story

  • Shuttle office needs CampusNav
  • At the end: merge into one

The campus shuttle office wants a simple program that helps riders check stops, distances, and delays. The class splits into 8 teams of one. Each team owns exactly one function. Once every function works on its own, the whole class merges them into a single program: CampusNav.

Student 1: isValidStop()

Signature: bool isValidStop(int stop, int total)
Input: a stop index, and the total number of stops
Output: true if stop is a real index (0 to total-1)
Test cases:
isValidStop(3, 5) → true
isValidStop(5, 5) → false
isValidStop(-1, 5) → false
Only if. No loop needed.

bool isValidStop(int stop, int total) {
  if (stop < 0) return false;
  if (stop >= total) return false;
  return true;
}

Student 2: nextStop()

Signature: int nextStop(int cur, int total)
Input: the current stop index, and the total stops
Output: the next stop; wraps to 0 after the last one
Test cases:
nextStop(2, 5) → 3
nextStop(4, 5) → 0
Only if. No loop needed.

int nextStop(int cur, int total) {
  if (cur + 1 >= total) return 0;
  return cur + 1;
}

Student 3: stopType()

Signature: char stopType(int stop)
Input: a stop index, 0 through 9
Output: 'B' for 0-2, 'T' for 3-5, 'W' for 6-9
Test cases:
stopType(1) → 'B'
stopType(4) → 'T'
stopType(8) → 'W'
Only if. No loop needed.

char stopType(int stop) {
  if (stop < 3) return 'B';
  if (stop < 6) return 'T';
  return 'W';
}

Student 4: isRushHour()

Signature: bool isRushHour(int hr)
Input: the hour, 0 to 23
Output: true during 7-9 AM or 4-6 PM, else false
Test cases:
isRushHour(8) → true
isRushHour(17) → true
isRushHour(12) → false
Only if. No loop needed.

bool isRushHour(int hr) {
  if (hr == 7 || hr == 8 || hr == 9)
    return true;
  if (hr == 16 || hr == 17 || hr == 18)
    return true;
  return false;
}

Student 5: totalDistance()

Signature: int totalDistance(int dist[], int n)
Input: distances between consecutive stops, and n
Output: the sum of all n distances
Test cases:
totalDistance({2,4,3}, 3) → 9
Only while. No if needed.

int totalDistance(int dist[], int n) {
  int sum = 0;
  int i = 0;
  while (i < n) {
    sum += dist[i];
    i++;
  }
  return sum;
}

Student 6: buildCumulative()

Signature: void buildCumulative(int dist[], int cum[], int n)
Input: distances dist[], an empty array cum[], and n
Output: none; cum[i] holds distance to reach stop i
Test cases:
dist = {2,4,3} → cum = {2,6,9}
Only while. No if needed.

void buildCumulative(int dist[], int cum[],
                      int n) {
  int i = 0;
  int total = 0;
  while (i < n) {
    total += dist[i];
    cum[i] = total;
    i++;
  }
}

Student 7: reverseRoute()

Signature: void reverseRoute(int stops[], int n)
Input: the route as an array of stop IDs, and n
Output: none; reverses stops[] in place for the trip back
Test cases:
{1,2,3,4} → {4,3,2,1}
Only while. No if needed.

void reverseRoute(int stops[], int n) {
  int left = 0, right = n - 1;
  while (left < right) {
    int temp = stops[left];
    stops[left] = stops[right];
    stops[right] = temp;
    left++; right--;
  }
}

Student 8: printCountdown()

Signature: void printCountdown(int left)
Input: how many stops remain before arrival
Output: none; prints a line per stop, down to 1
Test cases:
printCountdown(3) prints 3, 2, 1
Only while. No if needed.

void printCountdown(int left) {
  while (left > 0) {
    std::cout << left
         << " stops left\n";
    left--;
  }
}

CampusNav: All Eight Merge

  • All 8 functions, one program
  • main() calls each in order
  • CampusNav is ready to ride

Deliverable

  • Write your one function
  • Test it against its cases
  • Merge and run CampusNav

Objects and Classes

What Is an Object?

Quick Example: Engine

  • Engine: under the hood
  • State: horsepower, cylinders
  • Behavior: start()
class Engine {
private:
  double horsepower;
  int cylinders;
public:
  void start();
};

Quick Example: Transmission

  • Transmission: shifts the gears
  • State: type, gears
  • Behavior: shift()
class Transmission {
private:
  string type;
  int gears;
public:
  void shift();
};

Quick Example: Battery

  • Battery: powers the car
  • State: voltage, cycleCount
  • Behavior: charge()
class Battery {
private:
  double voltage;
  int cycleCount;
public:
  void charge();
};

Quick Example: FuelTank

  • FuelTank: holds the gas
  • State: capacity, level
  • Behavior: refill()
class FuelTank {
private:
  double capacity;
  double level;
public:
  void refill();
};

Quick Example: Tire

  • Tire: meets the road
  • State: size, treadDepth

Objects Are Everywhere

  • A phone: a Contact object
  • A game: a Player object
  • A store app: a Cart object

Check: State or Behavior?

Is a car's color state or behavior? What about honk()?

color is state (something the car HAS). honk() is behavior (something the car DOES).

Questions?

Classes: The Blueprint

One Class, Many Objects

Step 1: An Empty Class

  • class is a new keyword
  • Car: the blueprint's name
  • Semicolon after the braces
class Car {

};

Step 2: Create Objects

  • Car: the type, like int
  • c1, c2: two Car objects
  • Each is separate and own data
Car c1;
Car c2;

Check: Class or Object?

Is Car a class or an object? Is c1 a class or an object?

Car is the class (the blueprint). c1 is an object (one actual car built from it).

Questions?

Member Variables

Member Variables = State

  • Each object's own data
  • Live inside the class body
  • One copy per object

Step 3: Add Member Variables

  • string for make and model
  • int for the year
  • double for mileage
class Car {
  string make;
  string model;
  int year;
  double mileage;
};

Step 4: Dot Notation

  • object.member: one field
  • Reads just like English
  • Each object, its own copy
c1.make = "Honda";
c1.year = 2024;
std::cout << c1.make;

Check: Separate Copies?

c1.year = 2024; c2.year = 2019;. What is c1.year now?

Still 2024. Each object has its own separate copy of every member variable.

Questions?

Constructors

Why a Constructor?

  • Without one: junk start data
  • A constructor runs on creation
  • Guarantees a valid start state

Step 5: A Constructor

  • Same name as the class
  • No return type at all
  • Runs once, when c1 is made
Car() {
  mileage = 0;
}

Step 6: Take Parameters

  • Pass in starting values
  • this->make avoids a clash
  • Sets all four fields at once
Car(string mk, string md, int yr) {
  make = mk;
  model = md;
  year = yr;
  mileage = 0;
}

Check: Which Runs First?

Car c1("Honda", "Civic", 2024);. When does the constructor run?

Immediately: the moment c1 is created, before any other line touches c1.

Step 7: Build an Object

  • Values go in the parentheses
  • Matches the constructor order
  • c1 starts fully set up
Car c1("Honda", "Civic", 2024);

Questions?

Member Functions

Behavior = Member Functions

  • Live inside the class too
  • Can read/change member vars
  • Called with dot notation

Step 8: drive() Function

  • void: returns nothing
  • Adds miles to mileage
  • Changes this object in place
void drive(double miles) {
  mileage += miles;
}

Step 9: getInfo() Function

  • Returns a formatted string
  • Reads this object's own fields
  • No parameters at all
string getInfo() {
  return make + " " + model;
}

Check: Whose Mileage?

c1.drive(50); c2.drive(10);. Does this change c1's mileage or c2's?

Each call only changes its own object. c1.drive(50) only updates c1.mileage.

Sample Run: Car Object

Questions?

Public vs Private

Why Hide Data?

  • mileage = -500 makes no sense
  • private blocks direct access
  • public methods control changes

Step 10: private / public

  • private: hidden from outside
  • public: the object's interface
  • Members default to private
class Car {
private:
  double mileage;
public:
  void drive(double m);
};

Step 11: A Safe Getter

  • Lets code read mileage
  • Still can't be set directly
  • Read-only, one-way access
double getMileage() {
  return mileage;
}

Check: Can It Compile?

mileage is private. Does c1.mileage = 10; outside the class compile?

No. Outside code cannot touch a private member directly, by design.

Extension: isNew()

Write isNew(), returning true when mileage is under 500.

bool isNew() {
  return mileage < 500;
}

Questions?

Practice Lab

Requirements: Dealership Tool

  • Track one car for sale
  • Record a test drive's miles
  • Print a one-line summary

Plan Your Class

Name the private fields and the two public functions this tool needs.

make, model, year, mileage (private). drive(miles) and getInfo() (public).

Step 1: Class Skeleton

  • Four private fields
  • public: starts the interface
  • Constructor comes next
class Car {
private:
  string make, model;
  int year;
  double mileage;
public:
};

Step 2: The Constructor

  • Takes make, model, year
  • mileage always starts at 0
  • Goes inside public:
Car(string mk, string md, int yr) {
  make = mk; model = md; year = yr;
  mileage = 0;
}

Step 3: drive()

  • Takes the miles driven
  • Adds onto mileage
  • Returns nothing
void drive(double miles) {
  mileage += miles;
}

Step 4: getInfo()

  • Builds one summary string
  • Combines make, model, miles
  • Returns it to the caller
string getInfo() {
  return make + " " + model
       + ", " + to_string(mileage);
}

Check: Why to_string()?

mileage is a double, but getInfo() returns a string. Why call to_string()?

You cannot add a double directly to a string with +; to_string() converts it first.

Step 5: Use the Class

  • Build one Car object
  • Simulate a test drive
  • Print the summary
Car c1("Honda", "Civic", 2024);
c1.drive(12.5);
std::cout << c1.getInfo();

Sample Run: Dealership Tool

Add a private double price, plus a getter getPrice().

private:
  double price;
public:
  double getPrice() {
    return price;
  }

Deliverable

  • Write the full Car class
  • Build one object, drive it
  • Print getInfo(), show output

Questions?

Practice Lab Part 2

The Scenario: Garage Manager

  • A small garage: 5 cars
  • Each one its own Car object
  • Report on the whole garage

The Plan: Array of Objects

Step 1: Declare the Array

  • fleet: 5 Car objects
  • Each already default-built
  • Same array syntax from Mod. 5
Car fleet[5];

Step 2: Fill the Array

  • Assign each slot a real car
  • Uses the constructor directly
  • Five distinct objects now
fleet[0] = Car("Honda", "Civic", 2024);
fleet[1] = Car("Ford", "F-150", 2021);

Step 3: Print the Garage

  • Loop every index, 0 to 4
  • fleet[i]: that one Car object
  • Call getInfo() on each
for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
  std::cout << fleet[i].getInfo();
}

Check: fleet[2].drive()

fleet[2].drive(30); : which car in the garage just changed?

Only the Car object at index 2. The other four are untouched.

Step 4: Find the Newest

  • Track the lowest mileage
  • Compare one object at a time
  • Reuses getMileage() from Mod.
int best = 0;
for (int i = 1; i < 5; i++) {
  if (fleet[i].getMileage() <
      fleet[best].getMileage())
    best = i;
}

Extension: Needs Service

Count how many cars in fleet have mileage over 5000.

int count = 0;
for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++)
  if (fleet[i].getMileage() > 5000)
    count++;

Deliverable

  • Fill the 5-car garage
  • Print every car's info
  • Report the newest car

What Is Inheritance?

What Is Inheritance?

  • A new class reuses an old one
  • Car IS-A Vehicle
  • No copy-pasting code twice

Why Not Just Copy-Paste?

  • Two classes, same fields twice
  • Fix one, forget the other
  • Inheritance: one true source

Check: IS-A or HAS-A?

A Car has an Engine. A Car is a Vehicle. Which relationship is inheritance?

IS-A. Car is a Vehicle uses inheritance. Car has an Engine is composition, a member variable instead.

Base and Derived Classes

Step 1: The Base Class

  • Vehicle: shared fields
  • make, model, year
  • Every vehicle has these
class Vehicle {
public:
  string make, model;
  int year;
};

Step 2: A Derived Class

  • : public Vehicle means IS-A
  • Car gets make/model/year free
  • Plus its own new field
class Car : public Vehicle {
public:
  int doors;
};

Step 3: Use the Derived Class

  • c has make, model, year, doors
  • Inherited fields work directly
  • No extra code needed
Car c;
c.make = "Honda";
c.doors = 4;

Check: What Does Truck Get?

class Truck : public Vehicle. Does Truck have a make field?

Yes. Truck inherits every public member of Vehicle automatically, including make.

Protected Members

private vs protected vs public

  • private: this class only
  • protected: class + children
  • public: anyone

Step 4: Use protected

  • mileage: visible to Car, Truck
  • Still hidden from outside code
  • The middle ground of the three
class Vehicle {
protected:
  double mileage;
public:
  string make, model;
};

Check: Can Car Reach It?

mileage is protected in Vehicle. Can a Car member function read mileage directly?

Yes. protected is visible inside the class itself and any class that inherits from it.

Overriding Functions

Same Name, New Behavior

  • Vehicle has a describe()
  • Car can define its own version
  • Car's version runs for a Car

Step 5: Base Version

  • Generic, works for any vehicle
  • Returns a plain description
  • Car can replace this
string describe() {
  return "A vehicle";
}

Step 6: Override in Car

  • Same name, same return type
  • Defined again, inside Car
  • Runs for Car objects now
string describe() {
  return "A car";
}

Check: Which Version Runs?

Car c; c.describe();. Does this call Vehicle's describe() or Car's?

Car's. When Car defines its own describe(), it replaces (overrides) Vehicle's for Car objects.

Constructors in Inheritance

Base Runs First

  • Vehicle's own ctor runs first
  • Then Car's own constructor
  • Base is always set up first

Step 7: Pass to the Base

  • Vehicle(mk, md) : runs first
  • Car adds doors on top
  • Colon syntax calls the base
Car(string mk, string md, int d)
  : Vehicle(mk, md) {
  doors = d;
}

Check: Order of Execution

Car c("Honda", "Civic", 4);. Which constructor body runs first: Vehicle's or Car's?

Vehicle's. The base class is always fully constructed before the derived class body runs.

More Derived Classes

Step 8: A Second Derived Class

  • Truck also IS-A Vehicle
  • Gets make, model, mileage
  • Adds its own towCapacity
class Truck : public Vehicle {
public:
  double towCapacity;
};

One Base, Many Children

  • Car and Truck both reuse it
  • Each adds its own extra field
  • Fix Vehicle once, both benefit

Check: Fix in One Place

A bug in Vehicle's mileage logic is fixed inside Vehicle itself. Does Truck need its own fix too?

No. Truck inherits Vehicle's code, not a copy of it, so the one fix in Vehicle covers Truck automatically.

Practice Lab

Requirements: Dealership Fleet

  • Vehicle: make, model, year
  • Car adds doors
  • Truck adds towCapacity

Step 1: Vehicle Base

  • protected mileage
  • public make, model, year
  • A describe() to override later
class Vehicle {
protected:
  double mileage;
public:
  string make, model;
  int year;
};

Step 2: Car and Truck

  • Both inherit from Vehicle
  • Car adds doors
  • Truck adds towCapacity
class Car : public Vehicle {
public: int doors;
};
class Truck : public Vehicle {
public: double towCapacity;
};

Step 3: Build Both Objects

  • Each gets make/model/year free
  • Plus its own extra field
  • Two distinct types, one base
Car c;
c.make = "Honda"; c.doors = 4;
Truck t;
t.make = "Ford"; t.towCapacity = 5000;

Check: Shared or Separate?

c.make and t.make: do they share one variable, or does each object have its own?

Each object has its own separate copy of make, exactly like any other member variable.

Deliverable

  • Write Vehicle, Car, Truck
  • Build one of each
  • Print both, show they differ

Practice Lab Part 2

Scenario: Override describe()

  • Vehicle::describe() is generic
  • Car and Truck each override it
  • Same call, different wording

Step 1: Override in Car

  • Car's own describe()
  • Mentions doors specifically
  • Replaces Vehicle's version
string describe() {
  return "A car with " +
    to_string(doors) + " doors";
}

Step 2: Override in Truck

  • Truck's own describe()
  • Mentions towCapacity instead
  • A third, different wording
string describe() {
  return "A truck that tows " +
    to_string(towCapacity);
}

Extension: Motorcycle

Add a third class, Motorcycle, with its own hasSidecar and its own describe().

class Motorcycle : public Vehicle {
public: bool hasSidecar;
};

Check: Three Calls, Three Answers

c.describe(); t.describe(); m.describe();. Do all three print the same text?

No. Each class overrides describe() with its own version, so each object prints its own wording.

Deliverable

  • Override describe() x3
  • Build one of each class
  • Show all 3 outputs

Word Origin: "Inheritance"

Latin Root
  • "Heres," an heir
  • Legal term, passing property
Simula, 1967
  • Borrowed for a subclass
  • getting a base class's traits

A derived class "inherits" its base class's members the same way a child inherits from a parent: the metaphor is deliberate, borrowed straight from family law.

What Is Polymorphism?

What Is Polymorphism?

  • Greek: poly + morph
  • One call, many behaviors
  • Depends on the real object

Check: Overriding or Polymorphism?

Writing Car's own describe() is overriding. What is it called when one line of code picks the right one at runtime?

Polymorphism. Overriding sets up the different versions; polymorphism is choosing the right one automatically.

Virtual Functions

Why virtual Matters

  • No virtual: base version runs
  • With virtual: real object wins
  • One keyword changes everything

Step 1: Mark It virtual

  • virtual goes in the base class
  • Signals: children may override
  • Only needs it once, in Vehicle
class Vehicle {
public:
  virtual string describe() {
    return "A vehicle";
  }
};

Check: Where Does virtual Go?

Does virtual need to be repeated on Car's own describe(), or only on Vehicle's?

Only on Vehicle's. Once a function is virtual in the base class, every override stays virtual automatically.

Pointers to the Base Class

A Base Pointer, Many Objects

  • Vehicle* points to any child
  • Legal, since Car IS-A Vehicle
  • The pointer stays Vehicle*

Step 2: Point at a Car

  • Vehicle* holds a Car's address
  • &c: the address-of operator
  • Legal because Car IS-A Vehicle
Car c;
Vehicle* v = &c;

Check: Is This Legal?

Truck t; Vehicle* v = &t;. Is this legal, given Truck also inherits from Vehicle?

Yes. Any class that inherits from Vehicle can have its address stored in a Vehicle pointer.

Calling Through a Pointer

Step 3: Call Through v

  • v->describe() uses an arrow
  • virtual runs Car's version
  • Not Vehicle's version
Vehicle* v = &c;
std::cout << v->describe();
// prints Car's version

Without virtual: The Old Behavior

  • No virtual: always Vehicle's
  • The pointer type wins here
  • This is why virtual matters

Check: Same Call, Different Object

Vehicle* v; v points first at a Car, then at a Truck. Does v->describe() print the same thing both times?

No, if describe() is virtual: it prints Car's version first, then Truck's, matching the real object each time.

Abstract Classes

A Class You Can Never Build

  • = 0 means pure virtual
  • No body at all in Vehicle
  • Every child MUST provide one

Step 4: A Pure Virtual Function

  • = 0 instead of a body
  • Vehicle becomes abstract
  • Only children can be built
class Vehicle {
public:
  virtual string describe() = 0;
};

Check: What Must Car Do Now?

Vehicle::describe() is pure virtual. What happens if Car does not define its own describe()?

Car itself becomes abstract too, and cannot be built, until it provides its own describe().

Arrays of Base Pointers

One Array, Mixed Objects

  • Vehicle* fleet[3]
  • Each slot: any real type
  • Loop once, every type handled

Step 5: Build the Array

  • Three different real types
  • All stored as Vehicle pointers
  • One array holds them all
Car c;
Truck t;
Motorcycle m;
Vehicle* fleet[3] = {&c, &t, &m};

Step 6: Loop and Call

  • One loop, three outputs
  • Picks the real describe()
  • Polymorphism, in practice
for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
  std::cout << fleet[i]->describe();
}

Check: Three Calls, One Line

The loop above runs fleet[i]->describe() for i = 0, 1, 2. Does it print the same text three times?

No. Each slot points at a different real object, so each call prints that object's own describe().

Practice Lab

Requirements: Make describe() virtual

  • Start from Module 8's classes
  • Add virtual to describe()
  • Car/Truck still override it

Step 1: Mark Vehicle Virtual

  • Just one keyword added
  • No other code needs to change
  • Car, Truck already override
class Vehicle {
public:
  virtual string describe() {
    return "A vehicle";
  }
};

Step 2: Build Three Objects

  • One Car, Truck, base pointer
  • Point it at each in turn
  • Call describe() each time
Car c;
Truck t;
Vehicle* v = &c;
std::cout << v->describe();
v = &t;
std::cout << v->describe();

Check: Prove It Is Real

How could you prove to a classmate that this is really calling Car and Truck's own versions, not Vehicle's?

Make Vehicle's own text obviously different, like "A vehicle (base)", and show it never actually prints.

Deliverable

  • Add virtual to Vehicle
  • Point at Car, then Truck
  • Show both real versions print

Practice Lab Part 2

Scenario: The Whole Fleet, Polymorphically

  • An array of Vehicle pointers
  • Car, Truck, Motorcycle, mixed
  • One loop, every real type

Step 1: Build the Fleet Array

  • One of each real vehicle type
  • Stored as Vehicle pointers
  • The array type never changes
Car c;
Truck t;
Motorcycle m;
Vehicle* fleet[3] = {&c, &t, &m};

Step 2: Print the Whole Fleet

  • One loop handles every type
  • No if/else needed at all
  • Polymorphism, not branching
for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++)
  std::cout << fleet[i]->describe()
       << "\n";

Extension: Add a Fourth Type

Add an RV class with its own describe(), then add it to the fleet array.

class RV : public Vehicle {
public:
  string describe() {
    return "An RV";
  }
};

Check: Why No if/else?

The loop in Step 2 never checks what type each fleet[i] really is. Why does it still print the right thing?

Because describe() is virtual: the correct version runs automatically based on the real object, no if/else needed.

  • Build the 3-vehicle fleet
  • Loop, print every describe()
  • Show one output per real type

Lab 1

Lab 1: Getting Started

  • Answer in your own words
  • A few sentences per question
  • No prior experience needed

Question

What do you think a "computer program" actually is?

Answer

Something a computer runs using its internal components, where the code gets read by the hardware.

Question

Have you ever used an app or website that didn't work right? What happened?

Answer

A Minecraft mod turned the screen black. Only one specific, worse-performing setting fixed it, so the mod got removed.

Question

What's different about talking to a person versus "talking" to a computer?

Answer

A person shows body language and tone. Talking to a computer is more like talking at it, since you only get text back.

Question

If you had to tell a computer, step by step, how to make a sandwich, what would you need to say?

Answer

Every step, explicitly: get plates and bread, spread the filling, then place one slice on top so they touch.

Question

Just from the word itself, what do you think "debugging" means?

Answer

Removing bugs from a program so it functions correctly.

Question

Why do you think computers need such exact, precise instructions?

Answer

It's like how there, their, and they're sound the same but mean different things. A computer can't guess which one is meant.

Question

Have you ever followed confusing instructions or a recipe? What made them hard to follow?

Answer

Helped build a PC over the summer; ports and wires were named differently across manuals, and some parts had no instructions at all.

Question

Name one app you use every day. What do you think it's doing behind the scenes?

Answer

Reddit: it tracks votes, calculates karma, lets people post, and sorts content by popularity and growth potential.

Question

If a program you wrote didn't do what you expected, how would you start figuring out why?

Answer

Read the compiler's error output line by line, then double-check the logic by testing again.

Question

What's one thing you'd like to be able to build by the end of this course?

Answer

Card games are a hobby, so building a virtual version of one would be fun to try.

Question

What applications are low-level languages used for today?

Answer

Anything close to the hardware or needing top speed: operating-system kernels, device drivers, and embedded chips.

Example: the Linux kernel and Arduino firmware are written in C.

Question

Why do run-time errors occur?

Answer

The code compiled fine, but while running it reaches a case it cannot handle, like bad input or dividing by zero.

Example: 10 / n compiles, then crashes when the user types n = 0.

Question

What is the difference between an error and a bug?

Answer

The bug is the mistake in your code. The error is what the computer reports when that bug runs. Fix the bug, the error goes away.

Example: = instead of == is the bug; the wrong output is the error.

Question

Why was the original language named "C"?

Answer

It followed a Bell Labs language called B, so Dennis Ritchie named the next step C, the next letter.

Example: the lineage is BCPL to B to C, and later C++ (one past C).

Please read the course syllabus and ask any questions; once completed, confirm you have read the syllabus.

Homework 1

Homework 1: Evolution of C++

  • Part 1: confirm syllabus read
  • Part 2: read C++ paper, 10 Qs

Reading: Bjarne Stroustrup, The Evolution of C++: 1985 to 1989 (first four pages)

Question

  • Why the name C++?
  • Who is Stroustrup?
  • Why 1985?

Answer

"++" is the increment operator: one better than C. Stroustrup built it at Bell Labs (AT&T) starting in 1979, released it publicly in 1985.

Covered in: Module 1

Question

  • Stable, but evolving?
  • Why avoid unportable code?
  • Why not easier for beginners?

Answer

Stable means old code keeps compiling as new features are added. Portability and full power mattered more than an easy on-ramp.

Covered in: Module 1

Question

  • Abstraction vs. OOP?
  • What is a class?

Answer

Data abstraction hides how a type is built behind a clean interface. OOP adds inheritance and polymorphism on top. A class is C++'s tool for both.

Covered in: Module 7

Question

  • Hardest goal to balance?
  • What do safe/efficient mean?

Answer

Safe means hard to misuse; efficient means fast and low-memory. The two often pull against each other, which is why balancing them is hardest.

Covered in: Module 6–7

Question

  • What is type-safe linkage?
  • What does overloading do?

Answer

Type-safe linkage lets the compiler catch mismatched calls across separately-compiled files. Overloading lets one function name serve many types.

Covered in: Module 6

Question

  • Why add multiple inheritance?
  • What's an abstract class?

Answer

Single inheritance only extends one parent; some designs need two. An abstract class defines an interface with no full implementation of its own.

Covered in: Module 8

Question

  • Why skip these in the paper?
  • What are they?

Answer

Both were still being designed in 1989, so the paper only covers shipped C++ 2.0 features. Exceptions handle runtime errors; templates write one type for many kinds of data.

Covered in: Module 11

Question

  • What's a static member?
  • What does operator-> do?

Answer

A static member belongs to the class, not to any one object. operator-> lets a custom "smart pointer" type use ordinary pointer syntax.

Covered in: Module 7–8

Question

  • Has C++ changed since 1989?
  • Why is this so hard to read?

Answer

Yes, hugely; C++11 through C++23 each added major features. This paper is a design memo for other language experts, not a tutorial. Read it for the "why," not to fully understand every term yet.

Covered throughout the course

Reading: Think C++, Chapter 4 (Runestone Academy)

Question

Q1. Briefly describe a situation where if/else or switch is needed to decide an outcome.

Answer

A login screen needs if/else to decide whether to grant access, show an error, or lock the account, since the outcome depends entirely on which condition is true.

Question

Q2. Why would you prefer switch instead of if/else statements?

Answer

A switch reads more clearly when one variable is compared against many exact values, since it avoids repeating that variable's name in every single condition.

Question

Q3. What does "break" do?

Answer

break exits the switch statement right away, so execution jumps past the closing brace instead of falling through into the next case's code.

Question

Q4. What is the "default" statement used for in switches?

Answer

default runs when none of the listed case values match, giving the program a defined behavior for input it did not explicitly plan for.

Question

Q5. Briefly describe what this code snippet does.

if (isRaining || isSnowing) {
    std::cout << "bring an umbrella";
} else {
    std::cout << "you don't need one!";
}

Answer

It checks whether it is raining or snowing. If either is true, it prints a message recommending an umbrella; if both are false, it prints a message saying one is not needed.

Question: 25 pts

  • Ask the user about weather
  • Rain: take an umbrella
  • Cold: wear a jacket
  • Hot: bring water
  • Else: you're good to go
  • Use if / else if / else

Answer

string w;
cin >> w;
if (w == "rain") cout << "Take umbrella.";
else if (w == "cold") cout << "Wear jacket.";
else if (w == "hot") cout << "Bring water.";
else cout << "You're good to go!";

Run it: OnlineGDB C++ Compiler

Question: 25 pts

  • Rebuild Q1 using switch/case
  • 1=Rain 2=Cold 3=Hot 4=Other

Answer

int w;
cin >> w;
switch (w) {
  case 1: cout << "Take umbrella."; break;
  case 2: cout << "Wear jacket."; break;
  case 3: cout << "Bring water."; break;
  default: cout << "Good to go!";
}

Run it: OnlineGDB C++ Compiler

Question: 25 pts

int score = 85;
if (score >= 60) {
  cout << "You passed.";
}
else if (score >= 80) {
  cout << "B or higher.";
}
else {
  cout << "Did not pass.";
}

Answer

// 60 is checked FIRST, so it
// prints "passed" and skips
// the B-or-higher check
if (score >= 80)
  cout << "B or higher.";
else if (score >= 60)
  cout << "You passed.";
else
  cout << "Did not pass.";
